kg.node.rt_radial_shear.in.strength: How far the coordinates are dragged.
kg.node.rt_radial_shear.in.offset: A shift applied after the distortion.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.desc.1: Converts a uv into polar form around a center: x becomes the distance from the center and y becomes the angle around it.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.desc.2: Sampling a texture with the result wraps it into a ring, which is how radial wipes, sonar sweeps and vortex effects are usually built.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.in.uv: Coordinates to convert; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.in.center: The pole everything is measured from.
kg.node.rt_polar_coordinates.note.1: The angle wraps from 1 back to 0 on one side of the center; a texture sampled across that line shows a visible seam.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.desc.1: Remaps a uv into a single cell of a sprite sheet, so one texture can hold a whole animation. Drive tile from Time to play it.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.uv: Coordinates within the cell; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.width: Number of columns in the sheet.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.height: Number of rows in the sheet.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.in.tile: Which cell to show. It wraps automatically, so a value that keeps growing simply loops.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.option.invertX.toolt: Traverse the columns right to left.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.option.invertY.toolt: Traverse the rows bottom to top.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.example.1: Floor of Time * 12 into tile plays a 4x4 sheet at twelve frames a second.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.note.1: Cells bleed into each other when the sampler filters across their edges. Point filtering, or a sheet with padding, avoids it.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.desc.1: Projects a texture onto the surface along all three world axes and blends the three samples by the normal — so geometry gets a consistent texture with no uv at all, and no stretching or seams.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.desc.2: Unconnected position and normal default to the mesh's model-space position and world normal, and an unconnected texture falls back to the missing-texture sampler.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.in.position: Point being textured; unconnected uses the mesh position.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.in.normal: Surface normal driving the blend; unconnected uses the mesh normal.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.in.blend: Sharpness of the transition between the three projections.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.1: Three texture fetches per pixel instead of one.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.2: The default position is model space while the default normal is world space. That agrees for an unrotated mesh; wire matching-space inputs if the mesh rotates.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.3: Fragment-only, since it samples a texture.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.option.type.tooltip: Default: blend the three samples as color.
Normal: treat the samples as normal maps and blend them into a world-space normal.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.4: Type Normal is the one normal-mapping path that needs no mesh tangent at all - it builds its basis from the three projection axes. That makes it the reliable choice in the vertex stage, or on a mesh whose UV cannot anchor a tangent basis.
kg.node.rt_triplanar.note.5: The output port stays Vector4 in Normal mode; the normal rides in XYZ, and wiring it into a Vector3 input truncates to XYZ for you.
kg.node.rt_texture.desc.1: Names a texture and its sampler settings. The compiler bakes it into the material as its own sampler uniform, so this is a constant with no runtime cost.
kg.node.rt_texture.desc.2: It outputs a sampler handle rather than a color — feed it into Sampler Texture 2D to actually read a pixel.
kg.node.rt_texture.note.1: Filter and wrap live in this node's settings, not on the sampling node — set Repeat here if you plan to tile the coordinates.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.desc.1: Reads a pixel out of a sampler at the given coordinates. The one node that turns a texture into a color.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.in.sampler: Where to read from; unconnected falls back to the missing-texture checkerboard.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.in.uv: Where to read; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_sampler_texture2d.example.1: Texture into sampler, and Sampler Texture 2D into Base Color, reproduces an ordinary textured render type.
kg.node.rt_overlay_texture.desc.1: Minecraft's overlay sampler — the red flash on a hurt entity and the white flash on a creeper about to explode.
kg.node.rt_overlay_texture.desc.2: Using this node tells the runtime to bind vanilla's overlay texture. Sample it with the UV1 channel.
kg.node.rt_lightmap_texture.desc.1: Minecraft's lightmap sampler — the baked block and sky light that gives world geometry its lighting.
kg.node.rt_lightmap_texture.desc.2: Using this node tells the runtime to bind vanilla's lightmap. Sample it with the UV2 channel and multiply the result into your base color.
kg.node.rt_lightmap_texture.note.1: The Vertex Color node's Block mode already does this for you; reach for this node only when you want the lightmap on its own.
kg.node.rt_screen_position.desc.1: Where this fragment sits on the screen, in the coordinate space you pick. The default mode is the canonical uv to feed Scene Color and Scene Depth.
kg.node.rt_screen_position.out.out: The screen position; which channels are meaningful depends on the mode.
kg.node.rt_screen_position.note.1: Fragment-only. Because it is screen-space, anything built on it slides across the surface as the camera moves.
kg.node.rt_screen.desc.1: The viewport size in pixels. Use it to correct for aspect ratio, or to turn a pixel measurement into a fraction of the screen.
kg.node.rt_screen.example.1: Dividing Width by Height gives the aspect ratio, which keeps a screen-space circle round instead of oval.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.desc.1: The color of the opaque scene already drawn behind this fragment. This is what makes refraction, heat haze and frosted glass possible.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.desc.2: Offsetting the uv slightly before sampling is exactly how a refraction distortion is built: the surface shows the world behind it, displaced.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.in.uv: Screen-space coordinates to read; unconnected uses this fragment's own screen position.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.out.out: The scene color behind this fragment.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.note.1: Only meaningful for a translucent material. The capture is taken after all opaque geometry, so an opaque material draws before the capture exists and reads nothing.
kg.node.rt_scene_color.note.2: The editor preview shows black — the capture happens during the world render, which does not run behind the offscreen preview scene. It is correct in-world.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.desc.1: How far away the opaque scene behind this fragment is. Comparing it against the fragment's own depth is what softens the edge where a particle or a water plane meets solid geometry.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.in.uv: Screen-space coordinates to read; unconnected uses this fragment's own screen position.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.out.out: The depth, in the units the sampling mode implies.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.example.1: Saturate of the difference between Scene Depth in eye mode and Screen Position raw's w, divided by a fade distance, gives the classic soft-particle fade.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.note.1: Only meaningful for a translucent material, for the same reason as Scene Color.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.note.2: The editor preview shows a flat value — there is no scene depth behind the offscreen preview. It is correct in-world.
kg.node.rt_camera.desc.1: The current camera's position, orientation and clip planes — Unity's Camera node.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Position: Absolute world position of the camera.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Direction: The direction the camera looks, in world space.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Up: The camera's up axis, in world space.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Right: The camera's right axis, in world space.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.Orthographic: 1 for an orthographic projection, 0 for perspective.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.NearPlane: Near clip distance in world units.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.FarPlane: Far clip distance in world units.
kg.node.rt_camera.out.ZBufferSign: 1 in this pipeline: depth grows away from the camera.
kg.node.rt_camera.example.1: Camera Right and Up let a quad face the camera without any billboarding on the CPU side.
kg.node.rt_camera.note.1: Position is reassembled from KilaGraph's precision-split camera uniforms, so it stays accurate far from the world origin.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's global shader uniforms, straight from the source. Most of these have a friendlier node — Camera, Screen, Game Time — so reach for this one when you need something they do not expose.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.CameraBlockPo: Integer block part of the camera position, in the precision split.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.CameraOffset: Fractional part of the camera position, in the precision split.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.GlintAlpha: Strength of the enchantment glint overlay.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.out.MenuBlurRadiu: Blur radius the pause menu is applying.
kg.node.rt_globals_ubo.note.1: Add CameraBlockPos and CameraOffset to get the world camera position — or just use the Camera node, which does it for you.
kg.node.rt_projection_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's projection matrix, which turns view space into clip space.
kg.node.rt_dynamic_transforms_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's per-draw transform uniforms — the values vanilla sets before each draw call.
kg.node.rt_dynamic_transforms_ubo.out.Co: The per-draw color tint vanilla multiplies in.
kg.node.rt_dynamic_transforms_ubo.out.Te: Texture coordinate matrix, used by animated render types.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.desc.1: The space-conversion matrices KilaGraph precomputes each draw. They let a graph do its own space math instead of going through the Transform node.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.out.IModelV: View space back to object space.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.out.IViewMa: View space back to world space.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.out.IProjMa: Clip space back to view space.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.note.1: Referencing an output is what declares and binds the matching uniform, so unused matrices cost nothing.
kg.node.rt_kg_transforms_ubo.note.2: The camera's world position is not here — use the Camera node for that.
kg.node.rt_projection_from_position.desc: Applies the projection matrix to a position, taking it into clip space.
kg.node.rt_projection_from_position.in.p: The view-space position; unconnected falls back to the model-space vertex position.
The clip-space position, before the perspective divide.
kg.node.rt_projection_from_position.note: Vertex-only: clip space is a per-vertex concept, and this feeds gl_Position.
kg.node.rt_lighting_ubo.desc.1: The two directional lights vanilla uses for its per-vertex diffuse shading.
kg.node.rt_lighting_ubo.note.1: These are fixed directions in view space, not real world lights — vanilla entity lighting is deliberately simple.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.desc.1: Vanilla's per-vertex diffuse lighting, exposed as a node. This is the shading that used to be hidden inside the Color block; the default entity shader now wires it explicitly so you can edit or remove it.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.in.normal: Surface normal; unconnected uses the Normal vertex attribute.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.in.color: Color to light; unconnected uses the Color vertex attribute.
kg.node.rt_mix_light.note.1: Vertex-only, because its unconnected fallbacks are vertex attributes.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.desc.1: Blends a color toward the fog color by distance — the last step of a render type that should disappear into the distance like the rest of the world.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.desc.2: Every input except inColor is optional: unconnected, each falls back to the value vanilla would have used, so wiring only inColor already reproduces vanilla fog.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.sphericalVertexD: Distance driving the fog; unconnected uses the standard fog distance.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.environmentalSta: Distance at which fog begins; unconnected uses vanilla's FogStart.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.environmentalEnd: Distance at which fog is total; unconnected uses vanilla's FogEnd.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.fogColor: Color to fade toward; unconnected uses vanilla's FogColor.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.note.1: 1.21.1 has a single linear fog band. The cylindrical and render-distance ports are kept for graph compatibility with newer versions but do not affect the result here.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.desc.1: Minecraft's fog uniforms, for building a custom fog response instead of using Apply Fog.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogColor: The color the world fades toward.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogRenderDistance: Same band as environmental on this version.
Same band as environmental on this version.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogSkyEnd: Same band as environmental on this version.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.out.FogCloudsEnd: Same band as environmental on this version.
kg.node.rt_fog_ubo.note.1: 1.21.1 exposes a single fog band, so the multi-band outputs all report that one band. They exist so a graph stays compatible with newer versions.
kg.node.rt_linear_fog_value.desc.1: How much fog applies at a given distance: 0 before the start, rising to 1 at the end. Use it when you want to drive something other than color with fog.
kg.node.rt_total_fog_value.desc.1: The fog amount for this fragment using the scene's own fog settings — Linear Fog Value with everything filled in for you.
kg.node.rt_total_fog_value.example.1: One Minus of this, multiplied into Alpha, fades a render type out with distance instead of tinting it.
kg.node.rt_fog_spherical_distance.desc.1: Vanilla's spherical fog distance for a position: the straight-line distance from the camera, which is what standard fog uses.
kg.node.rt_fog_spherical_distance.in.pos: The position to measure; unconnected uses the model-space vertex position.
kg.node.rt_fog_spherical_distance.note.1: Vertex-only. Vanilla computes fog distance per vertex and interpolates it; read it in the fragment stage with the Frag Spherical Vertex Distance node.
kg.node.rt_fog_cylindrical_distance.desc: Vanilla's cylindrical fog distance: horizontal distance and height treated separately, which is how the void and nether fogs behave.
kg.node.rt_fog_cylindrical_distance.in.p: The position to measure; unconnected uses the model-space vertex position.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.desc.1: A two-color checker over the uv. It is derivative-aware, so the squares stay crisp and stop shimmering as they shrink into the distance instead of turning into noise.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.in.colorA: Color of the first set of squares.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.in.frequency: How many squares per uv unit on each axis.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.note.1: Fragment-only, because the anti-aliasing needs screen-space derivatives.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.desc.1: Soft fractal value noise in 0..1: three octaves of a hashed lattice summed together, so it has both broad shapes and fine detail.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.in.scale: Base frequency. Higher means smaller features.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.example.1: Add Time to the uv before the noise and it drifts; multiply the result into Alpha for a dissolving effect.
kg.node.rt_simple_noise.note.1: Value noise is blockier than gradient noise. When you want smooth organic shapes, Gradient Noise is the better choice.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.desc.1: Perlin-style gradient noise: random directions at each lattice corner, dotted with the local offset and blended with a quintic fade, then biased into 0..1.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.desc.2: Smoother and more organic than Simple Noise, which is why it is the usual starting point for clouds, smoke and flowing distortion.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_gradient_noise.example.1: Two Gradient Noises at different scales, one offsetting the other's uv, gives the classic swirling distortion.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.desc.1: Worley noise: one feature point is scattered into each cell of a grid, and every pixel finds its nearest. The result reads as organic cells — cracked mud, scales, stained glass.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.in.angleOffset: Jitters where each cell's point sits. Animating it makes the cells crawl.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.in.cellDensity: How many cells fit across a uv unit.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.out.out: Distance to the nearest feature point: 0 at the point, approaching 1 at the cell borders.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.out.cells: A flat random value per cell — a per-region id, useful for coloring each cell differently.
kg.node.rt_voronoi.example.1: One Minus of out, raised to a high power, draws bright veins along the cell borders.
kg.node.rt_ellipse.desc.1: A mask that is 1 inside an axis-aligned ellipse centered on the uv and 0 outside, with a one-pixel anti-aliased edge that holds up at any zoom.
kg.node.rt_ellipse.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_ellipse.note.1: Fragment-only: the anti-aliased edge is sized with a screen-space derivative.
kg.node.rt_rectangle.desc.1: A mask that is 1 inside an axis-aligned rectangle centered on the uv, with an anti-aliased edge.
kg.node.rt_rectangle.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_rectangle.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_rounded_rectangle.desc.1: A rectangle mask with rounded corners, anti-aliased. The radius is clamped so it can never exceed half the shorter side.
kg.node.rt_rounded_rectangle.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_rounded_rectangle.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_polygon.desc.1: A mask of a regular polygon centered on the uv, with an anti-aliased edge.
kg.node.rt_polygon.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_polygon.in.sides: Number of sides. Three gives a triangle, six a hexagon; large values approach a circle.
kg.node.rt_polygon.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.desc.1: A regular polygon whose corners are rounded off by an arc, anti-aliased. Built on an exact signed distance field, so the rounding is a true offset of the shape rather than an approximation.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.in.uv: Coordinates; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.in.roundness: How much of each corner is replaced by an arc.
kg.node.rt_rounded_polygon.note.1: Fragment-only, like the other shape masks.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.desc.1: Rebuilds each output channel as a weighted mix of the input's red, green and blue. The three weight vectors default to the identity, so an unwired node passes the color through unchanged.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.in.red: How much R, G and B go into the output's red.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.in.green: How much R, G and B go into the output's green.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.in.blue: How much R, G and B go into the output's blue.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.example.1: Setting all three weight vectors to (0.33, 0.33, 0.33) gives a flat greyscale.
kg.node.rt_contrast.desc.1: Pushes colors away from mid-grey, or pulls them toward it. 1 leaves the color alone, above 1 hardens it, below 1 flattens it, and 0 collapses everything to grey.
kg.node.rt_contrast.note.1: The pivot is linear mid-grey, not 0.5, so the result matches what an image editor would do.
kg.node.rt_hue.desc.1: Rotates the color around the hue wheel, leaving how bright and how vivid it is untouched. Converts to HSV, shifts the hue, converts back.
kg.node.rt_hue.in.offset: The shift in degrees; it wraps, so 360 is a full turn back to the start.
kg.node.rt_hue.example.1: Time * 60 into offset cycles a color through the whole spectrum every six seconds.
kg.node.rt_invert_colors.desc.1: Inverts the channels you select and leaves the rest alone. The mask is per channel: 1 inverts, 0 keeps.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.desc.1: Swaps one color for another wherever the input is close enough to it — a chroma key. Everything outside the range is left untouched.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.in.to: The color to put in its place.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.in.range: How far from the target still counts as a match.
kg.node.rt_replace_color.in.fuzziness: How softly the replacement fades out past the range. 0 gives a hard cut.
kg.node.rt_saturation.desc.1: Pushes each channel away from the color's own brightness, or toward it. 1 leaves it alone, 0 gives greyscale, and above 1 oversaturates.
kg.node.rt_saturation.note.1: Brightness uses the Rec.709 weights, so green counts far more than blue — that is what keeps a desaturated image looking natural.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.desc.1: Warms or cools the image and shifts it between green and magenta, the same two controls a photo editor gives you.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.desc.2: It works by picking a white point and rebalancing in cone-response space rather than scaling RGB directly, which is why skin tones and neutrals survive the shift.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.in.temperature: Roughly -1 to 1. Positive warms toward orange, negative cools toward blue.
kg.node.rt_white_balance.in.tint: Roughly -1 to 1, shifting between green and magenta.
kg.node.rt_blend.desc.1: Combines two colors with a Photoshop-style blend mode, then fades from the base toward the result by opacity.
kg.node.rt_blend.desc.2: The mode is chosen at compile time, so only the formula you picked ends up in the shader — there is no runtime branch to pay for.
kg.node.rt_blend.in.opacity: How much of the blended result to apply. 0 gives the base back.
kg.node.rt_blend.note.1: Results are not clamped, matching Unity. Follow with Saturate if a mode can push channels out of range.
kg.node.rt_dither.desc.1: Subtracts a 4x4 ordered pattern that depends on the pixel's screen position. On its own it does almost nothing visible — the point is what happens when you threshold the result afterwards.
kg.node.rt_dither.desc.2: Thresholding a dithered value turns a smooth gradient into a stable screen-door pattern instead of a hard edge, which is how cutout fades and transparency-without-blending are usually done.
kg.node.rt_dither.example.1: Dither an alpha value and feed it into Alpha Discard for a fade that needs no blending and sorts correctly.
kg.node.rt_dither.note.1: Fragment-only, and the pattern is locked to screen pixels — so it stays put while the object moves behind it.
kg.node.rt_channel_mask.desc.1: Zeroes the channels you do not select. The mask is per channel: 1 keeps, 0 drops.
kg.node.rt_color_mask.desc.1: Produces a 0..1 mask that is 1 wherever the input is close to a target color, falling off past the range. The selection half of Replace Color.
kg.node.rt_color_mask.in.range: How far from the target still counts as a match.
kg.node.rt_color_mask.in.fuzziness: How softly the mask fades past the range.
kg.node.rt_normal_unpack.desc.1: Turns a normal-map texture sample into a real normal. Normal maps store directions squeezed into 0..1, so they have to be expanded back to -1..1 before they mean anything.
kg.node.rt_normal_unpack.note.1: Sample the normal map with a linear (non-sRGB) texture, otherwise the gamma curve bends the directions.
kg.node.rt_normal_unpack.note.2: The result is in tangent space, which is not yet something you can light with. Feed it into Transform with Tangent to World and type Normal to land it on the actual surface.
kg.node.rt_normal_strength.desc.1: Scales how pronounced a tangent-space normal is. 1 leaves it alone, 0 flattens it to face straight out, and above 1 exaggerates the bumps.
kg.node.rt_normal_blend.desc.1: Combines two tangent-space normals into one, using the whiteout method — so layering a detail normal over a base normal keeps both sets of bumps instead of one flattening the other.
kg.node.rt_normal_blend.in.b: The detail normal layered on top.
kg.node.rt_normal_reconstruct_z.desc.1: Rebuilds a normal's z from its x and y. Two-channel normal maps drop z to save space because a unit vector's third component is implied by the other two.
kg.node.rt_normal_reconstruct_z.in.in: The x and y of the normal.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.desc.1: Derives a normal from a height value by looking at how fast it changes across the screen. No height texture needed — it works on any float, including procedural noise.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.in.strengt: How pronounced the resulting bumps are.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.note.1: A screen-space approximation: the slopes are measured in pixels, so the apparent bumpiness changes with distance and zoom.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.note.3: Output Space World runs the result through the surface tangent basis for you, so you do not need a Transform node on the end.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.option.spa: Output space of the normal: Tangent (raw) or World (pushed through the surface tangent basis).
Tangent: the raw result, for feeding other normal nodes.
World: ready to light with, no Transform node needed.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_height.note.4: World mode inherits the same screen-space approximation: the slopes come from pixels while the basis is anchored to the UV.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.desc.1: Builds a normal from a height texture by sampling it three times — at the uv and one small step along each axis — and crossing the two resulting slopes.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.desc.2: Unlike Normal From Height this measures in texture space, so the bumpiness stays consistent regardless of how far away the surface is.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.textur: The height texture; unconnected falls back to the missing-texture sampler.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.uv: Where to sample; unconnected uses the mesh uv.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.offset: How far apart the samples are taken, in uv units.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.in.streng: How pronounced the resulting bumps are.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.note.1: Three texture fetches per pixel, and fragment-only.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.note.2: Output Space World runs the result through the surface tangent basis for you, so you do not need a Transform node on the end.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.option.sp: Output space of the normal: Tangent (raw) or World (pushed through the surface tangent basis).
Tangent: the raw result, for feeding other normal nodes.
World: ready to light with, no Transform node needed.
kg.node.rt_normal_from_texture.note.3: Unlike Normal From Height the slopes here are measured in UV units - the same thing the tangent basis is anchored to - so World mode is exact rather than approximate.
kg.node.rt_parallax_mapping.desc.1: Fakes depth on a flat surface. It shifts the UV along the direction you are looking at the surface from, in proportion to a height map, so grooves appear to sink in and bumps to stand out as you move around them.
kg.node.rt_parallax_mapping.desc.2: Feed the shifted UV into everything that samples that surface - base color, the normal map, all of it - otherwise the layers slide apart.
kg.node.rt_parallax_mapping.in.heightmap: The height map; red channel, 1 is the surface and 0 is the bottom of the groove.
kg.node.rt_parallax_mapping.in.uv: UV to shift; unconnected uses the mesh UV.
kg.node.rt_parallax_mapping.in.amplitude: How deep the relief reads, in surface units. Keep it small - parallax exaggerates fast.
kg.node.rt_parallax_mapping.note.1: One sample, one shift: it reads the height where you started rather than where your eye actually lands, so it skews on steep relief and at grazing angles. Use Parallax Occlusion Mapping when that shows.
kg.node.rt_parallax_mapping.note.2: Fragment-only, and only as good as the tangent basis behind it - see the Tangent node.
kg.node.rt_parallax_occlusion_mapping.de: The accurate version of parallax. Instead of guessing once, it walks along your line of sight in small steps until it drops below the height map, then interpolates the exact crossing - so deep relief keeps its shape even when you look along the surface.
Feed the shifted UV into everything that samples that surface, exactly as with plain Parallax Mapping.
kg.node.rt_parallax_occlusion_mapping.in: The height map; red channel, 1 is the surface and 0 is the bottom of the groove.
UV to shift; unconnected uses the mesh UV.
How deep the relief reads, in surface units.
kg.node.rt_parallax_occlusion_mapping.op: How many steps the march takes. More steps means less stepping artifact on steep relief, and proportionally more texture fetches.
kg.node.rt_parallax_occlusion_mapping.no: Up to steps + 2 texture fetches per pixel. 64 steps across a large surface is a real cost - start at 16 and raise it only until the stepping stops showing.
Steps is a dropdown rather than an input so the loop is a compile-time constant and unrolls.
Fragment-only, and only as good as the tangent basis behind it - see the Tangent node.
kg.node.rt_colorspace_conversion.desc.1: Converts a color between RGB, Linear and HSV. Everything routes through display RGB as the hub, so any pair of spaces works.
kg.node.rt_colorspace_conversion.desc.2: HSV is the useful one for color work: its x channel is hue, y is saturation and z is value, so shifting a single channel does exactly what you would expect.
RGB: display space, what a color picker gives you.
Linear: physically linear light, correct for blending and lighting math.
RGB: display space, what a color picker gives you.
Linear: physically linear light, correct for blending and lighting math.
kg.node.rt_colorspace_conversion.note.1: The sRGB and Linear conversion uses the common gamma 2.2 approximation rather than the exact piecewise curve.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.desc.1: Reads a color out of a Gradient at a position between 0 and 1. Color keys and alpha keys are interpolated separately, and the gradient's own mode decides whether the steps blend or snap.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.in.gradient: The gradient to sample, from a Gradient node or a Gradient variable.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.in.time: Where to sample, 0 to 1; unconnected sweeps across the mesh uv's x so the preview shows the whole gradient.
kg.node.rt_sample_gradient.example.1: A Fresnel value into time turns a gradient into a rim color ramp.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.desc.1: Reads a float out of a Curve at a position between 0 and 1, remapped into the curve's own output range. The graphical way to shape a value without a chain of math nodes.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.in.curve: The curve to sample, from a Curve node or a Curve variable.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.in.time: Where to sample, 0 to 1; unconnected sweeps across the mesh uv's x so the preview shows the whole curve.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.out.value: The sampled value, inside the curve's range.
kg.node.rt_sample_curve.example.1: Drive time from a linear Time node and let the curve do the easing, instead of assembling one out of Pow and Smoothstep.
kg.node.exec_entry.desc.1: The entry point of a blueprint's execution flow. It has no inputs — the host calls into it — and a single next output that fires the rest of the chain.
kg.node.exec_entry.out.next: Fires once when the run begins.
kg.node.exec_noop.tooltip: Does nothing and passes the flow through.
kg.node.exec_noop.desc.1: A pass-through with no behaviour. Useful purely for the shape of a graph: a tidy fan-in point where several branches meet, or a stable anchor to hang a breakpoint on.
kg.node.exec_branch.tooltip: The if statement: fires one of two outputs based on a condition.
kg.node.exec_branch.desc.1: Pulls the condition, then fires exactly one of the two exec outputs. Unlike the data-side Select node, this is real control flow — the branch not taken never runs.
kg.node.exec_branch.out.trueExec: Fires when the condition is true.
kg.node.exec_branch.out.falseExec: Fires when the condition is false.
kg.node.exec_gate.tooltip: Passes the flow through only while enabled.
kg.node.exec_gate.desc.1: Forwards the flow when enabled is true and drops it otherwise. A Branch with nothing wired to its false side, in one node.
kg.node.exec_gate.in.enabled: The flow continues only while this is true.
kg.node.exec_toggle_gate.tooltip: A gate that remembers whether it is open: Enter passes through while it is, and Open, Close and Toggle set it.
kg.node.exec_toggle_gate.desc.1: Unreal's Gate. Flow into Enter continues out of Exit only while the gate is open; flow into Open, Close or Toggle changes the state and continues nowhere. Start Closed decides how it begins. Unlike Gate, which reads a boolean input every time and remembers nothing, this one is set by events — a door opened by one trigger and walked through by another.
kg.node.exec_toggle_gate.in.enter: Passes to Exit while the gate is open; dropped while it is closed.
kg.node.exec_toggle_gate.in.toggle: Opens a closed gate, closes an open one. Continues nowhere.
kg.node.exec_toggle_gate.out.exit: Fires for every Enter that found the gate open.
kg.node.exec_toggle_gate.option.startClo: Whether the gate begins closed, so something has to open it first.
kg.node.exec_do_once.tooltip: Passes the flow through the first time only, until Reset.
kg.node.exec_do_once.desc.1: Unreal's DoOnce: In continues out of Out once; every In after that is swallowed until flow reaches Reset, which arms it again. Start Closed makes it need a Reset before the first pass. The memory is per running graph — each instance of a script has its own.
kg.node.exec_do_once.in.in: Passes the first time, swallowed after that.
kg.node.exec_do_once.out.out: Fires on the first In since the last Reset.
Whether it begins used up, so a Reset has to open it before the first pass.
kg.node.exec_do_n.tooltip: Passes the flow through the first N times, until Reset; Counter says how many so far.
kg.node.exec_do_n.desc.1: Unreal's DoN: Enter continues out of Exit the first N times; after that it is swallowed until flow reaches Reset, which starts the count over. Counter is the number of passes so far, this one included — a combo counter, a limited-use ability, the third strike.
kg.node.exec_do_n.in.enter: Passes while fewer than N have passed since the last Reset.
kg.node.exec_do_n.in.reset: Starts the count over. Continues nowhere.
kg.node.exec_do_n.in.n: How many passes are allowed per Reset.
kg.node.exec_do_n.out.exit: Fires for each of the first N Enters.
kg.node.exec_do_n.out.counter: How many have passed so far, this one included; 0 after a Reset.
kg.node.exec_flip_flop.tooltip: Alternates between two outputs: A, then B, then A again.
kg.node.exec_flip_flop.desc.1: Unreal's FlipFlop: the first trigger fires A, the next B, and so on. Is A says which one this was, for the chain that follows. A toggle in one node — a light switch, a crouch key that stands you up again.
kg.node.exec_flip_flop.out.a: Fires on the first, third, fifth… trigger.
kg.node.exec_flip_flop.out.b: Fires on the second, fourth… trigger.
kg.node.exec_flip_flop.out.isA: True when A fired this time.
kg.node.exec_multi_gate.tooltip: Each trigger fires the next output that has not fired yet — in order, or at random.
kg.node.exec_multi_gate.desc.1: Unreal's MultiGate: In fires out1 the first time, out2 the next, and so on; with Random, an output not used yet is picked at random instead. Once every output has fired, In does nothing more — unless Loop starts the round over. Start Index (counting from 1; 0 keeps going from where it left off) picks the first output of a round; Reset forgets which have fired.
kg.node.exec_multi_gate.in.reset: Forgets which outputs have fired. Continues nowhere.
kg.node.exec_multi_gate.in.startIndex: Which output a round begins with, counting from 1; 0 continues from where it left off.
kg.node.exec_multi_gate.option.random.to: Pick an unused output at random rather than the next in order.
kg.node.exec_multi_gate.option.loop.tool: Once every output has fired, start the round over rather than stopping.
kg.node.exec_sequence.tooltip: Fires several outputs one after another, in order.
kg.node.exec_sequence.desc.1: Runs each output's chain to completion before starting the next, so the branches never interleave. That makes execution order something you can rely on, rather than an accident of how the engine happens to queue work.
kg.node.exec_sequence.desc.2: The outputs are named out1, out2 and so on; the option below decides how many there are.
kg.node.exec_sequence.option.outputs.too: How many outputs to fire, in order.
kg.node.exec_switch.tooltip: Fires one of N outputs chosen by an integer.
kg.node.exec_switch.desc.1: An N-way selector: selector 1 fires case1, 2 fires case2, and anything outside the range falls through to defaultExec. The usual way to build a state machine or a dispatch table.
kg.node.exec_switch.in.selector: Which case to fire, counting from 1.
kg.node.exec_switch.out.defaultExec: Fires when the selector matches no case.
kg.node.exec_switch.option.cases.tooltip: How many case outputs to offer.
kg.node.exec_switch.note.1: Cases are keyed by integer only. For string or enum dispatch, compare first and feed the index in.
kg.node.exec_for.tooltip: Counted loop: runs the body a fixed number of times.
kg.node.exec_for.desc.1: Fires body count times, publishing the current iteration on index, then fires completed once the loop finishes.
kg.node.exec_for.in.count: How many iterations to run. Zero or less skips the body entirely.
kg.node.exec_for.out.index: The current iteration, from 0 to count minus 1.
kg.node.exec_for.out.completed: Fires once, after the last iteration.
kg.node.exec_for.example.1: For with count 3, its body wired to Print and index wired to Print's value, logs 0, 1, 2.
kg.node.exec_for.note.1: Loops can nest: each keeps its own index, so an inner loop cannot clobber the outer one's.
kg.node.exec_foreach.tooltip: Loops over a list, one element at a time.
kg.node.exec_foreach.desc.1: Fires body once per element, exposing the element on item and its position on index, then fires completed.
kg.node.exec_foreach.in.list: The list to walk. An empty or missing list skips the body.
kg.node.exec_foreach.out.index: The current element's position, counting from 0.
kg.node.exec_foreach.out.completed: Fires once, after the last element.
kg.node.exec_while.tooltip: Loops while a condition stays true.
kg.node.exec_while.desc.1: Re-pulls the condition before every iteration, so anything the body changes is visible to the next test.
kg.node.exec_while.in.cond: Checked before each iteration; the loop stops as soon as it is false.
kg.node.exec_while.out.completed: Fires once the condition turns false, or the cap is hit.
Hard cap on iterations, so a condition that never turns false cannot hang the server.
kg.node.exec_while.note.1: The cap is a safety net, not a design tool. If a loop legitimately runs longer than the cap, raise it rather than relying on it to stop.
kg.node.exec_break.desc.1: Stops the innermost loop it sits inside and continues from that loop's completed output.
kg.node.exec_break.note.1: Placing it outside any loop is an error, reported when the graph runs.
kg.node.exec_continue.tooltip: Skips to the next iteration of the nearest enclosing loop.
kg.node.exec_continue.desc.1: Abandons the rest of the current iteration and starts the next one.
kg.node.exec_continue.note.1: Placing it outside any loop is an error, reported when the graph runs.
kg.node.exec_print.tooltip: Logs a value to the KilaGraph log.
kg.node.exec_print.desc.1: Writes the value to the log and remembers the most recent one, so tests and debugging tools can read it back without parsing log text. The blueprint equivalent of a print statement.
kg.node.exec_print.in.value: Anything. It is converted to text for the log.
kg.node.exec_assert.tooltip: Fails the run when a condition is not met.
kg.node.exec_assert.desc.1: Throws with the supplied message if the condition is false, and otherwise carries on. Use it to state an assumption you want caught loudly rather than silently producing a wrong result.
kg.node.exec_assert.in.condition: What must hold. False aborts the run.
kg.node.exec_assert.in.message: Text attached to the failure, so the log says what was expected.
kg.node.exec_set_var.tooltip: Writes a value into a graph variable.
kg.node.exec_set_var.desc.1: Stores the value under the named graph variable. Variables marked as outputs end up in the run's result map, which is how a blueprint hands data back to whatever invoked it.
kg.node.exec_set_var.note.1: Reading goes the other way, through a variable node on the data side — there is no Get Var exec node.
kg.node.exec_cache.tooltip: Computes a value once and reuses it for the rest of the run.
kg.node.exec_cache.desc.1: The first pull evaluates the input and stores the result; every later pull returns the stored copy. The value survives loop iterations, so an expensive computation that does not change can sit outside the work without being re-derived each time round.
kg.node.exec_cache.desc.2: It is a pure data node with no exec ports. To force a recompute, wire its ref output into a Cache Clear node.
kg.node.exec_cache.in.value: Evaluated once, on the first pull.
kg.node.exec_cache.out.ref: A handle to this cache, for Cache Clear.
kg.node.exec_cache.note.1: The cache lives for one run. A fresh run starts empty.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.tooltip: Invalidates a Cache node so it recomputes.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.desc.1: Clears the caches wired into ref, then continues. The next pull on those caches evaluates their input again.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.in.ref: Which caches to clear. Leaving it unwired is a harmless no-op.
kg.node.exec_cache_clear.note.1: The ref wire is followed structurally rather than evaluated — pulling it would run the very cache that is about to be cleared.
kg.node.flow_select.tooltip: Picks one of two values based on a condition.
kg.node.flow_select.desc.1: The data-side ternary: out is ifTrue when the condition holds, ifFalse otherwise.
kg.node.flow_select.desc.2: Both sides are evaluated regardless of the condition. This selects a value, it does not skip work — for that, use the exec Branch node.
kg.node.flow_select.in.ifTrue: Used when the condition is true.
kg.node.flow_select.in.ifFalse: Used when the condition is false.
kg.node.flow_select.option.type.tooltip: The type carried by ifTrue, ifFalse and out.
kg.node.logic_and.tooltip: True only when every input is true.
kg.node.logic_and.desc.1: Folds all its inputs together with logical and. The option below sets how many inputs there are, so one node covers any arity.
kg.node.logic_and.out.out: True when every input is true.
kg.node.logic_or.tooltip: True when at least one input is true.
kg.node.logic_or.desc.1: Folds all its inputs together with logical or.
kg.node.logic_or.out.out: True when any input is true.
kg.node.logic_xor.tooltip: True when an odd number of inputs are true.
kg.node.logic_xor.desc.1: Folds all its inputs with exclusive or. With two inputs that reads as they differ; with more, it is a parity check.
kg.node.logic_xor.out.out: True when an odd number of inputs are true.
kg.node.logic_not.desc.1: True becomes false and false becomes true.
kg.node.logic_equals.tooltip: True when all inputs are equal.
kg.node.logic_equals.desc.1: Compares every input against the others for equality. It works on any type, not just numbers, so it also compares strings, items and block positions.
kg.node.logic_equals.out.out: True when all inputs are equal.
kg.node.logic_equals.note.1: Comparing floats for exact equality is unreliable. Test whether their difference is small instead.
kg.node.cmp_neq.tooltip: True when the two values differ.
kg.node.cmp_neq.desc.1: The inverse of Equals, over any type.
kg.node.cmp_neq.out.out: True when the two values differ.
kg.node.cmp_lt.tooltip: True when a is less than b.
kg.node.cmp_lt.in.b: The value to compare it against.
kg.node.cmp_lt.out.out: True when a is less than b.
kg.node.cmp_lt.note.1: Whole numbers are compared as whole numbers, so two large counters one apart really do compare as one apart.
kg.node.cmp_le.tooltip: True when a is less than or equal to b.
kg.node.cmp_le.in.b: The value to compare it against.
kg.node.cmp_le.out.out: True when a is less than or equal to b.
kg.node.cmp_le.note.1: Whole numbers are compared as whole numbers, so two large counters one apart really do compare as one apart.
kg.node.cmp_gt.tooltip: True when a is greater than b.
kg.node.cmp_gt.in.b: The value to compare it against.
kg.node.cmp_gt.out.out: True when a is greater than b.
kg.node.cmp_gt.note.1: Whole numbers are compared as whole numbers, so two large counters one apart really do compare as one apart.
kg.node.cmp_ge.tooltip: True when a is greater than or equal to b.
kg.node.cmp_ge.in.b: The value to compare it against.
kg.node.cmp_ge.out.out: True when a is greater than or equal to b.
kg.node.cmp_ge.note.1: Whole numbers are compared as whole numbers, so two large counters one apart really do compare as one apart.
kg.node.math_add.desc.1: Adds its inputs together. The option below sets how many there are, so one node covers two operands or ten.
kg.node.math_add.out.out: The sum of every connected input.
kg.node.math_multiply.out.out: The product of every connected input.
kg.node.math_divide.note.1: Dividing by zero gives infinity or a not-a-number value, which then poisons everything downstream. Guard the divisor if it can reach zero.
kg.node.math_modulo.tooltip: The remainder of a divided by b.
kg.node.math_modulo.desc.1: What is left over after dividing. Handy for wrapping a counter into a range, or testing divisibility by comparing the result against 0.
kg.node.math_modulo.in.b: What to divide it by. Defaults to 1.
kg.node.math_modulo.note.1: A divisor of zero gives 0 rather than failing.
kg.node.math_modulo.note.2: The remainder takes the sign of a, so -1 modulo 8 is -1 and not 7. Add the divisor and take the remainder again if you need a result that is always positive.
kg.node.math_modulo.note.3: Whole numbers stay whole. Feed this a tick count, a counter or an id and the remainder is exact however large the input gets; feed it decimals and it works in decimals as it always did. The number you type into b goes along with whichever the wire chose.
kg.node.math_negate.desc.1: Positive becomes negative and negative becomes positive.
kg.node.math_negate.out.out: The input with its sign flipped.
kg.node.math_abs.desc.1: Drops the sign, so -3 and 3 both give 3.
kg.node.math_abs.in.in: The number to take the magnitude of.
kg.node.math_sign.desc.1: Reports which side of zero the input is on, without its magnitude.
kg.node.math_sqrt.desc.1: The square root of the input.
kg.node.math_sqrt.in.in: The number to take the root of.
kg.node.math_pow.tooltip: base raised to the power exp.
kg.node.math_pow.desc.1: Exponentiation. An exp of 0.5 is the square root; 2 squares the base.
kg.node.math_pow.out.out: base raised to the power exp.
kg.node.math_exp.tooltip: e raised to the power of the input.
kg.node.math_exp.desc.1: The natural exponential. Growth that compounds — the inverse of the natural logarithm.
kg.node.math_log.tooltip: Logarithm of the input, in a chosen base.
kg.node.math_log.desc.1: The power the base must be raised to in order to give the input. The base defaults to e, the natural logarithm.
kg.node.math_log.note.1: An input of zero or less yields 0 rather than failing.
kg.node.math_log.in.in: The value to take the logarithm of.
kg.node.math_log.out.out: The logarithm of the input in the given base.
kg.node.math_log_base.tooltip: Logarithm of a value in an arbitrary base.
kg.node.math_log_base.desc.1: Computed as log(value) divided by log(base), so any base works.
kg.node.math_log_base.in.value: The number to take the logarithm of.
kg.node.math_log_base.out.out: The logarithm of value in the given base.
kg.node.math_min.desc.1: Picks the smallest value. With two inputs it also serves as an upper bound.
kg.node.math_max.desc.1: Picks the largest value. With two inputs it also serves as a lower bound — the cheap way to keep a number above zero.
kg.node.math_clamp.tooltip: Keeps a value inside a range.
kg.node.math_clamp.desc.1: Returns the input, or the nearest end of the range when it falls outside.
kg.node.math_clamp.out.out: The input, held inside the range.
kg.node.math_fract.tooltip: The part after the decimal point.
kg.node.math_fract.desc.1: Always lands in 0 up to but not including 1, so any input wraps into the unit range. The usual way to make a value repeat.
kg.node.math_fract.in.in: The number to take the fractional part of.
kg.node.math_fract.out.out: The part after the decimal point, always from 0 up to but not including 1.
kg.node.math_lerp.tooltip: Blends from a to b by t.
kg.node.math_lerp.desc.1: Linear interpolation: t of 0 gives a, 1 gives b, and values in between blend proportionally.
kg.node.math_lerp.note.1: t is not clamped, so values outside 0 to 1 extrapolate beyond a and b.
kg.node.math_remap.tooltip: Rescales a value from one range into another.
kg.node.math_remap.desc.1: Maps fromMin onto toMin and fromMax onto toMax, keeping everything in between proportional.
kg.node.math_remap.in.toMin: What the input range's start maps to.
kg.node.math_remap.in.toMax: What the input range's end maps to.
kg.node.math_remap.example.1: Remapping a 0 to 100 health value into 0 to 1 turns it straight into a bar fill fraction.
kg.node.math_remap.note.1: An input range of zero width is degenerate; the node returns toMin rather than dividing by zero.
kg.node.math_remap.out.out: The value rescaled into the output range.
kg.node.math_atan2.tooltip: The angle of the point (x, y), in radians.
kg.node.math_atan2.desc.1: The two-argument arctangent. Because it knows both coordinates it covers the full turn, which plain arctangent cannot — that is what makes it the right tool for turning an offset into a heading.
kg.node.math_atan2.example.1: Atan2 of the difference between a target and an entity gives the yaw to face it.
kg.node.math_atan2.out.out: The angle in radians, covering the full turn from -pi to pi.
kg.node.math_trig.tooltip: A trigonometry function, picked from a dropdown.
kg.node.math_trig.desc.1: One node covering the six common trigonometry functions. All of them work in radians.
kg.node.math_trig.option.op.tooltip.TAN: TAN: tangent; it blows up every half turn.
kg.node.math_trig.option.op.tooltip.ASIN: ASIN: the angle whose sine is the input, defined on -1 to 1.
kg.node.math_trig.option.op.tooltip.ACOS: ACOS: the angle whose cosine is the input, defined on -1 to 1.
kg.node.math_trig.option.op.tooltip.ATAN: ATAN: the angle whose tangent is the input.
kg.node.math_trig.in.in: The angle in radians, or the ratio for the inverse functions.
kg.node.math_trig.out.out: The result of the chosen function.
kg.node.math_angle_convert.desc.1: Every trigonometry node here works in radians, while Minecraft's own rotations are usually in degrees — this is the bridge between them.
kg.node.math_angle_convert.out.out: The same angle in the other unit.
kg.node.math_round.tooltip: Rounds to a whole number, in a chosen direction.
kg.node.math_round.desc.1: One node covering the four ways of dropping a fractional part.
kg.node.math_round.option.op.tooltip.ROU: ROUND: to the nearest whole number.
kg.node.math_round.out.out: The rounded value, still a float.
kg.node.math_random.tooltip: A random number between min and max.
kg.node.math_random.desc.1: Draws from the executor's shared generator, including min but excluding max.
kg.node.math_random.note.1: The roll is cached per node for one run, so reading the output twice gives the same number. To get a fresh roll each loop iteration, clear the cache or re-run.
kg.node.math_random.out.out: A random number in the range, min included and max excluded.
kg.node.math_random_int.tooltip: A random whole number between min and max.
kg.node.math_random_int.desc.1: Includes min and excludes max, so min 1 and max 7 rolls a six-sided die.
kg.node.math_random_int.note.1: When min equals max there is nothing to choose from, so the result is min.
kg.node.math_random_int.out.out: A random whole number, min included and max excluded.
kg.node.bitwise_and.desc.1: Keeps only the bits set in both inputs. The usual way to test or mask out flags.
kg.node.bitwise_and.example.1: value and 1 is 1 exactly when value is odd.
kg.node.bitwise_and.out.out: The bits that are set in both inputs.
kg.node.bitwise_and.note.1: Works on all 64 bits when either side is a long, and on 32 otherwise. So a packed position or an id keeps every bit, while a plain integer masks the way it always did.
kg.node.bitwise_or.desc.1: Sets a bit when either input has it. The usual way to combine flags.
kg.node.bitwise_or.out.out: The bits that are set in either input.
kg.node.bitwise_or.note.1: Works on all 64 bits when either side is a long, and on 32 otherwise.
kg.node.bitwise_xor.tooltip: Bitwise exclusive or of two integers.
kg.node.bitwise_xor.desc.1: Sets a bit where exactly one input has it. Applying the same value twice returns the original, which is what makes it a toggle.
kg.node.bitwise_xor.out.out: The bits that are set in exactly one of the inputs.
kg.node.bitwise_xor.note.1: Works on all 64 bits when either side is a long, and on 32 otherwise.
kg.node.bitwise_not.tooltip: Flips every bit of an integer.
kg.node.bitwise_not.desc.1: Inverts all 32 bits. On signed integers that turns n into -n minus 1, which surprises people expecting a plain sign flip.
kg.node.bitwise_not.out.out: The input with all 32 bits flipped.
kg.node.bitwise_not.note.1: Flips all 64 bits when the input is a long, and 32 otherwise.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_left.tooltip: Shifts the bits left, doubling per step.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_left.desc.1: Each step to the left multiplies by two. Bits shifted past the top are lost.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_left.in.bits: How many positions to shift by.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_left.note.1: Shifting a long moves within 64 bits, shifting anything else within 32. The distance wraps at that width, so shifting a 32-bit value by 35 is the same as shifting it by 3.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_right.tooltip: Shifts the bits right, halving per step.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_right.desc.1: Each step to the right halves the value, rounding toward negative infinity. The sign is preserved, so negative numbers stay negative.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_right.in.bits: How many positions to shift by.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_right.out.out: The shifted value, keeping its sign.
kg.node.bitwise_shift_right.note.1: Shifting a long moves within 64 bits, shifting anything else within 32. The distance wraps at that width, so shifting a 32-bit value by 35 is the same as shifting it by 3.
kg.node.convert_to_int.tooltip: Converts a number to a whole number.
kg.node.convert_to_int.desc.1: Takes any numeric wire and produces an integer, with the option below deciding what happens to the fractional part.
kg.node.convert_to_int.desc.2: The input accepts any type, so a float, a double or an int all connect. Anything that is not a number yields 0.
kg.node.convert_to_int.option.op.tooltip: How to drop the fractional part.
ROUND: to the nearest whole number.
kg.node.convert_to_int.out.out: The value as a whole number.
kg.node.convert_to_int.note.1: A value that is already whole is passed straight through, so the option only matters when there is a fractional part to drop.
kg.node.convert_to_int.note.2: An Int holds about two billion. A tick count, a packed position or an id will not fit, and this node stops at the limit rather than wrapping around — use To Long for those.
kg.node.convert_to_long.tooltip: Converts a number to a whole number, with room for large ones.
kg.node.convert_to_long.desc.1: The same as To Int, without the two-billion ceiling. This is the one for ticks, counters, ids and packed positions.
kg.node.convert_to_long.desc.2: It is also how you tell the math nodes that a number is whole. They pick how to calculate from what reaches them, so putting this in front of a value makes everything downstream of it exact instead of approximate.
kg.node.convert_to_long.option.op.toolti: How to drop the fractional part, when there is one.
kg.node.convert_to_long.out.out: The value as a whole number.
kg.node.convert_to_float.tooltip: Converts a number to a float.
kg.node.convert_to_float.desc.1: Accepts any numeric wire and widens it to a float. Anything that is not a number yields 0.
kg.node.convert_to_float.out.out: The value as a float, or 0 if it is not a number.
kg.node.convert_to_float.note.1: A float carries about seven significant digits. Converting a large whole number here rounds it to a nearby one — use To Double, or keep it whole with To Long.
kg.node.convert_to_double.tooltip: Converts a number to a double.
kg.node.convert_to_double.desc.1: Accepts any numeric wire and widens it to a double, which carries about sixteen significant digits instead of a float's seven. Anything that is not a number yields 0.
kg.node.convert_to_double.out.out: The value as a double, or 0 if it is not a number.
kg.node.convert_to_string.desc.1: Produces the value's textual form, which is what the string nodes and Print work with.
kg.node.convert_parse_number.tooltip: Reads a number out of text.
kg.node.convert_parse_number.desc.1: Parses the text as a number. Text that is not a number yields 0 rather than failing the run.
kg.node.convert_parse_number.desc.2: The text decides the kind of number: digits alone give a whole number and keep every digit of it, while a point or an exponent gives a decimal. So a pasted id or tick count arrives as the number you pasted.
kg.node.convert_parse_number.out.out: The parsed number, or 0 when the text is not one.
kg.node.convert_parse_bool.tooltip: Reads a boolean out of text or a number.
kg.node.convert_parse_bool.desc.1: The words true, yes and the digit 1 give true; anything else gives false. A number is true when it is not zero.
kg.node.convert_number_format.tooltip: Formats a number as text with a pattern.
kg.node.convert_number_format.desc.1: Renders the number using a decimal-format pattern, so you control the number of decimal places, thousands separators and the like.
kg.node.convert_number_format.option.pat: The decimal format pattern, for instance 0.00 or #,##0.
kg.node.convert_number_format.note.1: An invalid pattern falls back to the number's plain textual form instead of failing.
kg.node.convert_cast.tooltip: Asserts that a value is of a particular type.
kg.node.convert_cast.desc.1: Takes a wire of unknown type and re-labels it as the type you pick, which is how a generic output gets connected to a port that needs something specific.
kg.node.convert_cast.desc.2: This is the hinge of KilaGraph's unknown-type system: nodes such as list and map readers produce unknown values, and Cast is what tells the graph what they really are.
kg.node.convert_cast.option.targetType.t: The type the value is promised to be.
kg.node.convert_instanceof.option.target: The type to test against. An unset type accepts anything, matching the wire rule for UNKNOWN.
kg.node.convert_cast.note.1: The promise is checked when the graph runs. A value that does not fit fails the run rather than silently producing nonsense.
kg.node.list_combine.tooltip: Builds a list out of individual values.
kg.node.list_combine.desc.1: Gathers its inputs into a new list, in order. The type option decides what the elements are, and the input count decides how many there are.
kg.node.list_combine.option.type.tooltip: Element type of the list being built.
kg.node.list_combine.out.out: A new list holding the inputs, in order.
kg.node.list_range.tooltip: A list of numbers counting from one value to another.
kg.node.list_range.desc.1: Produces from, from plus step, and so on, stopping before it reaches to. The endpoint is excluded, so from 0 to 3 gives three entries.
kg.node.list_range.in.step: How much to advance each time.
kg.node.list_range.note.1: A step of zero or less would never terminate, so it yields an empty list instead.
kg.node.list_repeat.tooltip: A list holding the same value several times.
kg.node.list_repeat.desc.1: Repeats one value count times — a quick way to make a fixed-size list to fill in later.
kg.node.list_repeat.out.out: A list holding the value count times.
kg.node.list_size.tooltip: How many elements a list holds.
kg.node.list_is_empty.tooltip: True when a list has no elements.
kg.node.list_is_empty.desc.1: Equivalent to comparing Size against 0, in one node.
kg.node.list_is_empty.out.out: True when the list has no elements.
kg.node.list_get.tooltip: Reads the element at an index.
kg.node.list_get.desc.1: Fetches one element, counting from 0. The type option below decides what type the output claims to be, and the value is checked against it when the graph runs.
kg.node.list_get.option.type.tooltip: The type the element is expected to be.
kg.node.list_get.note.1: An index outside the list yields nothing rather than failing; pair it with Is Null if that case matters.
kg.node.list_index_of.tooltip: Where a value first appears in a list.
kg.node.list_index_of.desc.1: Returns the position of the first matching element, or -1 when it is absent.
kg.node.list_index_of.out.out: The position of the first match counting from 0, or -1 when absent.
kg.node.list_contains.tooltip: True when a list holds a value.
kg.node.list_contains.out.out: True when the value is present.
kg.node.list_append.tooltip: Adds a value to the end of a list.
kg.node.list_append.desc.1: Returns a new list with the value on the end.
kg.node.list_append.note.1: Like every list node here, this returns a new list rather than modifying the original — so wiring one list into two branches never lets one surprise the other.
kg.node.list_append.in.list: The list to start from. It is not modified.
kg.node.list_append.out.out: A new list with the value on the end.
kg.node.list_prepend.tooltip: Adds a value to the front of a list.
kg.node.list_prepend.desc.1: Returns a new list with the value at the start.
kg.node.list_prepend.in.list: The list to start from. It is not modified.
kg.node.list_prepend.out.out: A new list with the value at the front.
kg.node.list_insert.tooltip: Adds a value at a given position.
kg.node.list_insert.desc.1: Returns a new list with the value placed at the index, pushing later elements along.
kg.node.list_insert.in.index: Where to put it, counting from 0.
kg.node.list_insert.in.list: The list to start from. It is not modified.
kg.node.list_insert.out.out: A new list with the value at the given index.
kg.node.list_remove.tooltip: Removes the first occurrence of a value.
kg.node.list_remove.desc.1: Returns a new list with the first matching element dropped. A value that is not present leaves the list unchanged.
kg.node.list_remove.in.list: The list to start from. It is not modified.
kg.node.list_remove.out.out: A new list without the first match.
kg.node.list_remove_at.tooltip: Removes the element at an index.
kg.node.list_remove_at.desc.1: Returns a new list without that element.
kg.node.list_remove_at.in.index: Which element to drop, counting from 0.
kg.node.list_remove_at.in.list: The list to start from. It is not modified.
kg.node.list_remove_at.out.out: A new list without the element at that index.
kg.node.list_slice.tooltip: Takes a section out of a list.
kg.node.list_slice.desc.1: Returns the elements from one index up to but not including another.
kg.node.list_slice.note.1: Bounds outside the list are clipped rather than failing, and a from at or past to gives an empty list.
kg.node.list_slice.out.out: A new list holding the selected section.
kg.node.list_concat.tooltip: Joins several lists end to end.
kg.node.list_concat.desc.1: Produces one list containing every input's elements, in input order.
kg.node.list_concat.out.out: One list holding every input's elements.
kg.node.list_reverse.tooltip: Reverses the order of a list.
kg.node.list_reverse.desc.1: Returns a new list running back to front.
kg.node.list_reverse.out.out: A new list running back to front.
kg.node.list_distinct.desc.1: Keeps the first occurrence of each value and discards the rest, so the surviving order matches the original.
kg.node.list_distinct.out.out: A new list with duplicates dropped.
kg.node.list_sort.desc.1: Orders the elements naturally — numbers by value, text alphabetically.
kg.node.list_sort.option.ascending.toolt: On for smallest first, off for largest first.
kg.node.list_sort.note.1: Elements with no natural order are compared by their textual form, which is stable but rarely meaningful.
kg.node.list_sort.out.out: A new list in sorted order.
kg.node.map_create.tooltip: Builds a map from key and value pairs.
kg.node.map_create.desc.1: Gathers key1/value1, key2/value2 and so on into a map. Insertion order is preserved, so iterating the keys later gives them back in the order you wrote them.
kg.node.map_create.option.inputs.tooltip: How many key and value pairs.
kg.node.map_get.tooltip: Looks a key up in a map.
kg.node.map_get.desc.1: Returns the value stored under the key, or the fallback when the key is absent — so a missing entry never turns into a null halfway down the graph.
kg.node.map_get.in.defaultValue: Returned when the key is not present.
kg.node.map_get.out.value: The stored value, or the fallback.
kg.node.map_put.tooltip: Stores a value under a key.
kg.node.map_put.desc.1: Returns a new map with the entry added, replacing any existing value for that key.
kg.node.map_put.in.map: The map to start from. It is not modified.
kg.node.map_put.out.out: A new map including the entry.
kg.node.map_remove.tooltip: Deletes an entry from a map.
kg.node.map_remove.desc.1: Returns a new map without that key. A key that is absent leaves the map unchanged.
kg.node.map_remove.in.map: The map to start from. It is not modified.
kg.node.map_remove.out.out: A new map without that key.
kg.node.map_contains_key.tooltip: True when a map has a key.
kg.node.map_contains_key.desc.1: Tests for the key's presence without reading its value — which is how you tell a missing entry from one that is genuinely empty.
kg.node.map_contains_key.out.out: True when the key is present.
kg.node.map_contains_value.tooltip: True when a map holds a value.
kg.node.map_contains_value.desc.1: Scans every entry, so it is slower than a key lookup.
kg.node.map_contains_value.out.out: True when some entry holds the value.
kg.node.map_size.tooltip: How many entries a map holds.
kg.node.map_is_empty.tooltip: True when a map has no entries.
kg.node.map_is_empty.out.out: True when the map has no entries.
kg.node.map_keys.tooltip: All of a map's keys, as a list.
kg.node.map_keys.desc.1: Feed the result into For Each to walk the map.
kg.node.map_values.tooltip: All of a map's values, as a list.
kg.node.map_values.desc.1: The values in the same order as Keys, so the two line up index for index.
kg.node.map_merge.desc.1: Returns a new map holding every entry from both.
kg.node.map_merge.note.1: When both maps have the same key, b's value wins.
kg.node.map_merge.out.out: A new map holding every entry from both.
kg.node.optional_is_null.tooltip: True when a value is missing.
kg.node.optional_is_null.desc.1: Tests whether the wire carries nothing. Nodes that can fail to find something — a list index out of range, a block entity that is not there — report it this way.
kg.node.optional_is_null.out.out: True when the wire carries nothing.
kg.node.optional_not_null.tooltip: True when a value is present.
kg.node.optional_not_null.out.out: True when the wire carries a value.
kg.node.optional_default.tooltip: Substitutes a fallback when a value is missing.
kg.node.optional_default.desc.1: Passes the input through when it is present, and returns the fallback when it is not. One node instead of an Is Null feeding a Select.
kg.node.optional_default.in.in: The value that might be missing.
kg.node.optional_default.in.defaultValue: Used when the input is missing.
kg.node.optional_default.option.type.too: The type carried by both inputs and the output.
kg.node.string_length.tooltip: How many characters a string holds.
kg.node.string_concat.desc.1: Sticks its inputs end to end with nothing in between.
kg.node.string_concat.out.out: The inputs stuck end to end.
kg.node.string_format.tooltip: Builds a string from a pattern and arguments.
kg.node.string_format.desc.1: Substitutes the argument inputs into the pattern's placeholders. Better than a chain of Concat nodes whenever there is fixed text around the values.
kg.node.string_format.option.pattern.too: The pattern, with %s for text, %d for whole numbers and %.2f for two decimal places.
kg.node.string_format.option.inputs.tool: How many arguments the pattern takes.
kg.node.string_format.example.1: The pattern Health: %d/%d with two arguments produces text such as Health: 12/20.
kg.node.string_format.note.1: A pattern that does not match its arguments returns the pattern unchanged rather than failing the run.
kg.node.string_format.out.out: The pattern with its placeholders filled in.
kg.node.string_substring.tooltip: Takes a section out of a string.
kg.node.string_substring.desc.1: Returns the characters from one position up to but not including another.
kg.node.string_substring.note.1: Positions outside the string are clipped rather than failing, and a start at or past end gives empty text.
kg.node.string_substring.in.in: The text to take a section of.
kg.node.string_substring.out.out: The characters between the two positions.
kg.node.string_index_of.desc.1: Returns the position of the first match, or -1 when there is none.
kg.node.string_index_of.out.out: The position of the first match counting from 0, or -1 when there is none.
kg.node.string_contains.tooltip: True when one string appears inside another.
kg.node.string_contains.out.out: True when the substring occurs anywhere in the text.
kg.node.string_matches.tooltip: Whether a regular expression matches the whole string.
kg.node.string_matches.desc.1: Tests text against a pattern. The pattern has to cover the entire string, not merely appear somewhere inside it.
kg.node.string_matches.note.1: \d+ is true for 42 and false for x42. For a pattern that may sit anywhere, put .* on both ends, or use Regex Find, which also hands back what it matched.
kg.node.string_matches.note.2: A pattern with a syntax error answers false and says so on ok, rather than failing the run — the pattern is text somebody typed.
kg.node.string_matches.out.ok: False when the pattern is not valid regular expression syntax.
kg.node.string_find.tooltip: The first place a pattern matches, with its capture groups.
kg.node.string_find.desc.1: This is how text becomes data again. Run Command hands back a line of chat, and a pattern with parentheses turns "there are 3 of a max of 20" into two numbers.
kg.node.string_find.note.1: Searches from the front and stops at the first hit. Group 1 comes first in the list — the whole match already has its own port, so it is not repeated at the front.
kg.node.string_find.note.2: No match leaves start and end at -1 rather than 0, because 0 is a real position. A group that did not take part comes back as an empty string.
kg.node.string_find.note.3: Java's regex engine backtracks with no time limit, so a pattern like (a+)+b against a long non-matching string can hang. Possessive quantifiers such as a++ are the way out.
kg.node.string_find.out.end: One past where it ends, or -1. Feed both into Substring to cut around the match.
kg.node.string_find.out.ok: False when the pattern is not valid regular expression syntax.
kg.node.string_replace_regex.tooltip: Replaces every regex match, with $1 standing for a capture group.
kg.node.string_replace_regex.desc.1: Like Replace, except the search is a pattern and the replacement can refer back to what was captured: (\w+)=(\w+) with $2=$1 swaps both halves of every assignment in the text.
kg.node.string_replace_regex.note.1: A literal dollar sign or backslash in the replacement has to be preceded by a backslash. Getting that wrong, or naming a group the pattern does not have, reports on ok exactly as a bad pattern does.
kg.node.string_replace_regex.note.2: Count separates "changed nothing" from "matched nothing" without comparing strings. On failure the text passes through unchanged.
kg.node.string_replace_regex.in.replacem: What to put in place of each match. $1, $2 and so on stand for the capture groups.
kg.node.string_replace_regex.out.out: The text with every match replaced.
kg.node.string_replace_regex.out.ok: False when the pattern or the replacement is malformed.
kg.node.string_starts_with.tooltip: True when a string begins with another.
kg.node.string_starts_with.out.out: True when the text begins with the prefix.
kg.node.string_ends_with.tooltip: True when a string ends with another.
kg.node.string_ends_with.out.out: True when the text ends with the suffix.
kg.node.string_replace.tooltip: Swaps every occurrence of one substring for another.
kg.node.string_replace.desc.1: Replaces all matches, not just the first.
kg.node.string_replace.in.replacement: What to put in its place.
kg.node.string_replace.out.out: The text with every match replaced.
kg.node.string_split.tooltip: Breaks a string into a list at a delimiter.
kg.node.string_split.desc.1: Cuts the text wherever the delimiter appears and returns the pieces.
kg.node.string_split.note.1: The delimiter is plain text, not a pattern, so characters like . and | mean themselves.
kg.node.string_split.note.2: An empty delimiter has nothing to split on, so the result is a single-element list holding the original.
kg.node.string_split.out.out: The pieces, as a list of strings.
kg.node.string_join.tooltip: Joins a list into one string with a separator.
kg.node.string_join.desc.1: The counterpart to Split: puts the delimiter between consecutive elements.
kg.node.string_join.in.in: The list whose elements are joined.
kg.node.string_trim.desc.1: Strips leading and trailing spaces, tabs and newlines, leaving the inside alone.
kg.node.string_trim.out.out: The text without leading or trailing whitespace.
kg.node.string_case.tooltip: Changes the letter case of a string.
kg.node.string_case.desc.1: One node covering the three usual case conversions.
kg.node.string_case.option.op.tooltip.TI: TITLE: first letter of each word capitalised, the rest lowercase.
kg.node.string_case.out.out: The text in the chosen case.
kg.node.string_multiline.tooltip: A string literal written in a real text area.
kg.node.string_multiline.desc.1: A plain STRING constant gives you a one-line field, which is the wrong shape for the things graphs actually want to paste in — a UI XML document, a command block's worth of commands, a book page, a JSON payload. This node is the same string value with a proper editor over it: Enter starts a new line instead of committing.
kg.node.string_multiline.desc.2: The value is an ordinary string with a newline between the lines, so nothing downstream has to know it came from here. Feed it to Split with a newline delimiter to get the lines as a list.
kg.node.string_multiline.note.1: The text lives on the node, not on a wire — it is authored in the editor and saved with the graph, so there is no input port to override it at runtime.
kg.node.string_multiline.option.text.too: The text. Lines are joined with a newline.
kg.node.string_multiline.out.out: The whole text as one string.
kg.node.mc_block_to_item.desc.1: The item a block becomes when you pick it up. Blocks with no item form — fire, or the various technical blocks — give air instead.
kg.node.mc_item_to_block.desc.1: The block an item places. Items that place nothing give the air block, so check the result before using it.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_create.desc.1: Builds a stack from an item and a count. The count is not clamped to the item's stack limit here — the game decides what to do with an oversized stack when it is actually used.
kg.node.mc_item_in_tag.desc.1: Tests whether an item belongs to a tag — the game's own way of grouping things, so one check covers every kind of plank or every log rather than listing them by hand.
kg.node.mc_item_in_tag.in.tag: The tag id, for instance minecraft:planks.
kg.node.mc_item_in_tag.note.1: The tag is written as plain text. A malformed id gives false rather than failing the run.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_create.desc.1: Assembles a block position from three whole-number coordinates.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_offset.desc.1: Steps a position along a direction. The usual way to reach a neighbouring block without doing the coordinate arithmetic yourself.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_offset.in.amount: How many blocks. Negative values step the other way.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_offset.example.1: Offset by Up with an amount of 1 gives the block sitting directly on top.
kg.node.mc_get_block.desc.1: The block at a position in a level. It ignores the block's state, so a stair here is just the stair block, whichever way it faces.
kg.node.mc_get_block.note.1: The level has to come from a wire — a graph variable or a source node the host supplies. A missing level yields nothing rather than failing.
kg.node.mc_get_block_state.desc.1: The full block state at a position, including its properties: which way a stair faces, whether a door is open, how tall the grass is.
kg.node.mc_get_block_state.note.1: Use Get Block when you only care which block it is; this one when the properties matter.
kg.node.mc_get_block_entity.desc.1: The block entity at a position — the extra data attached to chests, furnaces, signs and the like.
kg.node.mc_get_block_entity.note.1: Most blocks have no block entity, so the result is often nothing. Guard it with Is Null.
kg.node.mc_is_empty_block.desc.1: True when there is nothing but air at that position.
kg.node.mc_entities_in_radius.desc.1: Every entity within a given distance of a point. Feed the result into For Each to act on all of them.
kg.node.mc_entities_in_radius.in.radius: How far to look, in blocks.
kg.node.mc_entities_in_radius.note.1: A large radius scans a lot of chunks. Keep it as small as the effect allows.
kg.node.mc_nbt_create.desc.1: A fresh, empty NBT compound to build up with Set.
kg.node.mc_nbt_get.desc.1: Reads one value out of an NBT compound by key. The value type option both decides how the raw tag is interpreted and what type the output claims to be.
kg.node.mc_nbt_get.option.valueType.tool: How to read the entry, and what type comes out.
BOOL: true or false, stored as a byte.
COMPOUND: a nested compound, for reading structures.
kg.node.mc_nbt_get.note.1: A missing key, or no tag at all, gives the type's default rather than failing — 0, empty text, or false.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.tooltip: Reads a value out of a compound by path, e.g. Inventory[0].id.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.desc.1: What NBT Get cannot do: that one takes a single key, so nested data needs a chain of reads and list elements are out of reach entirely. The syntax is the game's own, so anything /data get accepts works here.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.note.1: A path can match more than one tag — Inventory[].id matches every slot. Out is the first of them and count says how many there were, which is how a wildcard you did not mean shows itself.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.note.2: ok is about the path text, found is about the data: an unparseable path is ok false, while a good path that matched nothing is ok true and found false.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.note.3: Filters work too. Inventory[{id:"minecraft:stone"}].Count picks the slot out by its contents rather than by its index.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.out.out: The first match, read as the chosen type.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.out.count: How many tags the path matched.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.out.ok: False when the path is empty or not valid path syntax.
