kg.node.mc_nbt_path_get.option.valueType: How to read the value, and what type comes out.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.tooltip: Writes a value into a compound by path, e.g. display.Name.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.desc.1: Missing intermediate compounds are created on the way down, so writing a.b.c into an empty tag gives you all three — the same thing /data modify set does.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.note.1: A list slot that does not exist cannot be created: Items[4] on a three-element list writes nothing and reports count 0.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.note.2: Like NBT Set, this modifies the compound in place and hands the same one back rather than copying, so a second reader downstream sees the write. Chain writes onto one compound rather than branching off it.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.note.3: Count is how many matches were written, since a wildcard path can hit several at once.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.in.tag: The compound to write into. Passing nothing produces a fresh one.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.in.value: What to store; its type follows the option below.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.out.out: The compound, with the value written.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.out.ok: False when the path is malformed, or reached nothing that can hold a value.
kg.node.mc_nbt_path_set.option.valueType: The kind of value being stored.
kg.node.mc_nbt_set.desc.1: Writes a value into an NBT compound under a key, replacing whatever was there.
kg.node.mc_nbt_set.in.value: What to store; its type follows the option below.
kg.node.mc_nbt_set.option.valueType.tool: The kind of value being stored.
kg.node.mc_nbt_set.note.1: This modifies the compound in place and hands the same one back — unlike the list and map nodes, which always copy. Chain writes onto one compound rather than branching off it.
kg.node.mc_nbt_set.note.2: Passing nothing as the tag produces a fresh compound, so Set works as a one-node builder.
kg.node.mc_nbt_has.desc.1: True when the compound contains that key. Use it to tell a missing entry from one that holds a default-looking value.
kg.node.mc_nbt_remove.desc.1: Deletes a key from the compound and hands it back.
kg.node.mc_nbt_remove.note.1: Modifies the compound in place, like Set.
kg.node.mc_nbt_block_entity.desc.1: A block entity's saved data as an NBT compound — a chest's contents, a sign's text.
kg.node.mc_nbt_block_entity.note.1: The position and block id are not included, only the entity's own data.
kg.node.mc_entity_info.desc.1: Groups the readable properties of an entity: its coordinates, block position, name and whether it is alive.
kg.node.mc_entity_info.in.target: The entity every property block reads.
kg.node.mc_entity_position.tooltip: Where the entity is — its feet.
kg.node.mc_entity_position.desc.1: The point the game treats as the entity's location, at the bottom of its hitbox. For a line of sight use Eye Position instead.
kg.node.mc_entity_eye_position.tooltip: Where the entity is looking from.
kg.node.mc_entity_eye_position.desc.1: The start of a line of sight. Combine with Look Direction to cast a ray the way the entity is facing.
kg.node.mc_entity_look_direction.tooltip: The unit vector the entity is facing.
kg.node.mc_entity_look_direction.desc.1: Length 1, so scaling it gives a point that far ahead. Eye Position plus this times the reach is where the entity is aiming.
kg.node.mc_entity_look_direction.out.val: Unit vector along the entity's line of sight.
kg.node.mc_entity_velocity.tooltip: How fast the entity is moving, per tick.
kg.node.mc_entity_velocity.desc.1: Blocks per tick, as a vector — its length is the speed. Note this is the entity's own motion and does not include being carried by a vehicle.
kg.node.mc_entity_block_position.tooltip: The block the entity is standing in.
kg.node.mc_entity_block_position.desc.1: The entity's position floored to a block, the same rule the game uses to decide which block it occupies.
kg.node.mc_entity_block_position.out.val: The block coordinate the entity is in.
kg.node.mc_entity_bounding_box.tooltip: The entity's hitbox, in world space.
kg.node.mc_entity_bounding_box.desc.1: Already positioned, so it can be intersected against another box directly — no need to build one from the entity's position and type dimensions.
kg.node.mc_entity_rotation.tooltip: Where the entity is pointed, in degrees.
kg.node.mc_entity_rotation.desc.1: Yaw turns about the vertical axis; pitch tilts, and negative pitch is upward — the game's convention, not a mistake. Prefer Look Direction unless the angles themselves are wanted.
kg.node.mc_entity_rotation.out.yaw: Rotation about the vertical axis, in degrees.
kg.node.mc_entity_rotation.out.pitch: Tilt in degrees; negative looks up.
kg.node.mc_entity_identity.tooltip: The entity's network id, UUID and display name.
kg.node.mc_entity_identity.desc.1: The id is unique within a running world and is NOT stable across a restart. The UUID is stable and is what to store. The name is for showing to a player.
kg.node.mc_entity_identity.out.id: Network id — do not persist this.
kg.node.mc_entity_identity.out.name: The entity's display name.
kg.node.mc_entity_type.tooltip: What kind of entity this is.
kg.node.mc_entity_type.desc.1: Compare it against an Entity Type constant to test the kind, or feed it to Entity Type Properties for its hitbox size and category.
kg.node.mc_entity_state.tooltip: The entity's condition, as flags to branch on.
kg.node.mc_entity_state.desc.1: Together rather than one block each, because anything reacting to an entity asks several at once and a block per flag would mean six of them stacked to answer one question.
kg.node.mc_entity_state.out.alive: False once it has died or been removed.
kg.node.mc_entity_state.out.onGround: True when it is standing on something.
kg.node.mc_entity_state.out.inWater: True when its body is in water.
kg.node.mc_entity_state.out.invisible: True when it is not rendered.
kg.node.mc_entity_age.tooltip: How long the entity has existed, and how far it has fallen.
kg.node.mc_entity_age.desc.1: The tick count starts at zero when the entity is created, so it is how to make something happen a fixed time after a spawn. Fall distance resets on landing and is what fall damage is computed from.
kg.node.mc_entity_age.out.tickCount: Ticks since the entity was created.
kg.node.mc_entity_age.out.fallDistance: Blocks fallen since last on the ground.
kg.node.mc_entity_health.tooltip: Health and maximum health, for the entities that have any.
kg.node.mc_entity_health.desc.1: Health belongs to living entities — an arrow or a boat has none. Living says whether the numbers mean anything; when it is false they read zero rather than the block refusing to evaluate.
kg.node.mc_entity_health.note.1: Check Living before dividing health by max: for a non-living entity both are zero, and that is how a not-a-number reaches a health bar.
kg.node.mc_entity_health.out.living: True when this entity can have health at all.
kg.node.mc_player_info.desc.1: Groups the readable properties of a player — health, food level, experience level, whether they are in creative mode.
kg.node.mc_player_info.in.target: The player every property block reads.
kg.node.mc_player_food.desc.1: Food is the 0-to-20 bar. Saturation is the hidden reserve that drains before the bar does, which is why a player who just ate looks unchanged for a while. Exhaustion is the counter that consumes saturation as the player acts.
kg.node.mc_player_food.out.saturation: Hidden reserve consumed before the bar drops.
kg.node.mc_player_food.out.exhaustion: Counter that drains saturation as the player acts.
kg.node.mc_player_experience.tooltip: Level, bar progress and lifetime points.
kg.node.mc_player_experience.desc.1: Level is the number above the bar; progress is how full the bar is, 0 to 1; total is the lifetime points the score screen shows, and is not the sum of the other two.
kg.node.mc_player_experience.out.progres: How full the bar is, 0 to 1.
kg.node.mc_player_held_items.tooltip: What the player is holding in each hand.
kg.node.mc_player_held_items.desc.1: Either may be empty. Feed one into Unpack Item Stack to see what it is.
kg.node.mc_player_game_mode.tooltip: Whether the player is in creative, spectator, or may build.
kg.node.mc_player_game_mode.desc.1: As flags rather than a mode name, because that is how a graph uses it: the question is almost always whether this player may be affected by what is about to happen. Adventure reads as none of creative or spectator.
kg.node.mc_player_game_mode.out.canBuild: Whether the player may place and break blocks.
kg.node.mc_player_posture.tooltip: Whether the player is asleep or crouching.
kg.node.mc_player_posture.desc.1: Crouching is the visual state, which is also true when a player is forced low by a block above — it is not simply the sneak key.
kg.node.mc_player_posture.out.crouching: True while in the crouched pose.
kg.node.mc_level_info.desc.1: Groups the readable properties of a world: the time of day, the total game time, whether it is raining or thundering.
kg.node.mc_level_info.in.target: The world every property block reads.
kg.node.mc_level_rain_level.tooltip: How hard it is raining, 0 to 1.
kg.node.mc_level_rain_level.desc.1: Zero in clear weather, 1 in a downpour. Reads the fully-current value, the same one the server sees.
kg.node.mc_level_thunder_level.tooltip: How hard it is thundering, 0 to 1.
kg.node.mc_level_thunder_level.desc.1: Independent of the rain level, and both rise during a thunderstorm.
kg.node.mc_level_weather.tooltip: Whether it is raining, and whether it is storming.
kg.node.mc_level_weather.desc.1: Both in one block because they are not independent — a thunderstorm rains, so testing Raining alone catches storms too. Test Thundering when the difference matters.
kg.node.mc_level_weather.out.raining: True while it is raining or storming.
kg.node.mc_level_time.tooltip: The world clock: time of day, total age, and day or night.
kg.node.mc_level_time.desc.1: Day Time is the time of day and wraps every 24000 ticks. Game Time is the world's total age and never wraps — that is the one for anything that has to keep counting.
kg.node.mc_level_time.note.1: Day and Night are complements, so branching on one is branching on both.
kg.node.mc_level_time.out.dayTime: Time of day in ticks, wrapping every 24000.
kg.node.mc_level_time.out.gameTime: Total ticks since the world was created.
kg.node.mc_level_dimension.tooltip: Which dimension this level is, as an identifier.
kg.node.mc_level_dimension.desc.1: minecraft:overworld, minecraft:the_nether, minecraft:the_end, or whatever a datapack added. Compare it against an Identifier constant to branch on dimension.
kg.node.mc_level_bounds.tooltip: The vertical extent of the world, and its sea level.
kg.node.mc_level_bounds.desc.1: Not constants. A datapack can move them, and the Nether and End already differ from the Overworld — a graph iterating a column should read these rather than assume -64 to 320.
kg.node.mc_level_bounds.out.maxBuildHeig: One above the highest buildable Y.
kg.node.mc_level_bounds.out.seaLevel: The Y that water generates up to.
kg.node.mc_level_difficulty.tooltip: The world's difficulty, and whether it is hardcore.
kg.node.mc_level_difficulty.desc.1: The difficulty is its lower-case name — peaceful, easy, normal, hard — which is the form commands and datapacks use, so it compares directly against a text constant.
kg.node.mc_level_is_client.tooltip: Whether this level belongs to the client.
kg.node.mc_level_is_client.desc.1: The check to make before doing anything authoritative. A client level holds an approximation — entity lists are incomplete and block entities may be stubs — so writing game state from one is how desyncs are made.
kg.node.vector_make.tooltip: Builds a 3-component vector from three numbers.
kg.node.vector_make.desc.1: The inverse of Break Vector. An unconnected component reads zero, so wiring only X gives a vector along the X axis.
kg.node.vector_make2.tooltip: Builds a 2-component vector from two numbers.
kg.node.vector_make2.desc.1: Useful for anything flat: a texture coordinate, a point on the ground plane, a 2D offset.
kg.node.vector_make4.tooltip: Builds a 4-component vector from four numbers.
kg.node.vector_make4.desc.1: The usual reason for a fourth component is a colour with alpha, or a position carried through a projection.
kg.node.vector_break.tooltip: Splits a vector into its separate components.
kg.node.vector_break.desc.1: Reads whatever width arrives: a 2-component input leaves Z and W at zero, a 4-component one fills all four outputs.
kg.node.vector_break.out.z: The Z component, or zero if the input has none.
kg.node.vector_break.out.w: The W component, or zero if the input has none.
kg.node.vector_break.note.1: A component the input does not have reads zero rather than failing, so one node serves Vec2, Vec3 and Vec4.
kg.node.vector_add.tooltip: Adds two vectors component by component.
kg.node.vector_add.desc.1: Adding a vector is moving by it: a position plus a velocity is the next position.
kg.node.vector_add.in.b: The vector to add to it.
kg.node.vector_add.note.1: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_subtract.tooltip: Subtracts one vector from another, component by component.
kg.node.vector_subtract.desc.1: Subtracting positions gives the vector between them: target minus self points from you to the target, and its length is the distance.
kg.node.vector_subtract.note.1: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_scale.tooltip: Multiplies every component by one number.
kg.node.vector_scale.desc.1: Changes a vector's length without changing its direction. A negative factor reverses it; zero collapses it to the origin.
kg.node.vector_scale.in.scale: The factor every component is multiplied by. Defaults to 1, which leaves the vector alone.
kg.node.vector_scale.out.out: The scaled vector, same width as the input.
kg.node.vector_scale.note.1: Normalize then Scale is how you build a vector with a chosen direction and a chosen length.
kg.node.vector_dot.tooltip: Sum of the products of matching components.
kg.node.vector_dot.desc.1: Geometrically this is the length of a times the length of b times the cosine of the angle between them, so for two unit vectors it is exactly that cosine.
kg.node.vector_dot.desc.2: Positive means the two point broadly the same way, zero means they are perpendicular, negative means broadly opposite.
kg.node.vector_dot.out.out: The dot product, a single number.
kg.node.vector_dot.example.1: Dot a unit facing direction with a unit direction-to-target: 1 is straight ahead, 0 is directly to the side, -1 is directly behind. A cheap field-of-view test with no trigonometry.
kg.node.vector_dot.note.1: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_cross.tooltip: A vector perpendicular to both inputs.
kg.node.vector_cross.desc.1: Follows the right-hand rule: X crossed with Y gives Z. Its length is largest when the inputs are perpendicular and zero when they are parallel, so a zero result means the two are in line.
kg.node.vector_cross.example.1: Cross a surface normal with world up to get the direction running along the surface horizontally: the right vector of a wall.
kg.node.vector_cross.note.1: Genuinely three-dimensional, unlike the width-polymorphic majority of the group — which is why its pins are Vec3 rather than Vector. A 2- or 4-component input is read as its first three components.
kg.node.vector_length.desc.1: The straight-line length from the origin to the point the vector describes.
kg.node.vector_length.note.1: Merely comparing lengths does not need this node: dotting each vector with itself orders them the same way and skips a square root.
kg.node.vector_length.note.2: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_normalize.tooltip: Scales a vector to length 1, keeping its direction.
kg.node.vector_normalize.desc.1: Turns a vector into a pure direction, which is the form dot products and steering maths expect.
kg.node.vector_normalize.out.out: A vector of length 1 pointing the same way, or zero.
kg.node.vector_normalize.note.1: A zero-length vector normalizes to zero rather than to NaN. Dividing by its length would be a divide by zero, and one NaN spreads through every calculation downstream, so an unset direction stays harmless.
kg.node.vector_normalize.note.2: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_distance.tooltip: The straight-line distance between two points.
kg.node.vector_distance.desc.1: The same as taking the length of the difference, in one node.
kg.node.vector_distance.note.1: For a range check, comparing squared distances avoids the square root: Subtract, Dot the difference with itself, then compare against the radius squared.
kg.node.vector_distance.note.2: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_lerp.desc.1: At t = 0 the result is a, at t = 1 it is b, and in between it moves along the straight line joining them.
kg.node.vector_lerp.note.1: t is clamped to the 0 to 1 range, so this interpolates and never extrapolates past either end.
kg.node.vector_lerp.note.2: Blending two directions does not keep the length constant: the midpoint of two opposite unit vectors is zero. Normalize afterwards if you need a direction.
kg.node.vector_flatten.tooltip: Zeroes one component, leaving the others alone.
kg.node.vector_flatten.desc.1: Projects a vector onto a plane. Zeroing the up component turns a 3D velocity into just the part of it that moves along the ground.
kg.node.vector_flatten.out.out: The vector with the chosen component set to zero.
kg.node.vector_flatten.option.axis.toolt: Which component to zero: 0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z. Defaults to 1, because Y is up in Minecraft and flattening onto the ground plane is the common case.
kg.node.vector_flatten.example.1: Flatten a mob's velocity on Y, then take its Length, to get a horizontal speed that ignores falling.
kg.node.vector_flatten.note.1: An axis outside the input's width leaves the vector unchanged rather than failing.
kg.node.vector_yaw_between.tooltip: The signed turn in degrees from one direction to another, about the vertical axis.
kg.node.vector_yaw_between.desc.1: Answers how far you have to turn to face something. The sign says which way, so this is a turn to apply rather than just an angle between.
kg.node.vector_yaw_between.out.out: The turn in degrees, in the range -180 to 180.
kg.node.vector_yaw_between.example.1: Feed a mob's facing and its direction-to-target in, and the result can drive the turn directly: positive and negative already mean opposite ways round.
kg.node.vector_yaw_between.note.1: The result is folded into -180 to 180, so a turn of 350 degrees is reported as -10: always the shorter way round.
kg.node.vector_yaw_between.note.2: Uses Minecraft's yaw convention, where zero looks along +Z and positive turns toward -X. This matches the game's own rotation maths, so the value can be used as a yaw directly.
kg.node.vector_yaw_between.note.3: Only the horizontal components matter; the vertical one is ignored, so an input that also points up or down still gives a usable turn.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.tooltip: Rebuilds a vector by naming which component goes in each slot.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.desc.1: One node for reordering, narrowing, widening and repeating components. The mask names the source of each output slot in order, so xy takes the first two, zyx reverses, xxx repeats X three times, and xyz0 widens a Vec3 to a Vec4 with a zero on the end.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.desc.2: The mask decides the output width, which is what Break into Make cannot do: that pair always hands back a Vec3, whatever went in.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.in.in: The vector to read components from.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.out.out: A vector as wide as the mask is long.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.option.mask.toolt: Two to four characters from x, y, z, w, 0 and 1. Each names what the matching output slot holds: an axis of the input, or a literal zero or one.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.example.1: A Vec4 colour into a Vec3 with the alpha dropped: mask xyz. The same colour with red and blue swapped: mask zyx.
kg.node.vector_swizzle.note.1: An axis the input does not have reads zero, so xyzw on a Vec2 gives (x, y, 0, 0).
kg.node.vector_swizzle.note.2: A blank, malformed or one-character mask falls back to xyz. A single component is not a vector and could not be wired to anything downstream — use Get Component or Break Vector for that.
kg.node.vector_concat.tooltip: Lays several vectors end to end into one.
kg.node.vector_concat.desc.1: A Vec2 and another Vec2 give a Vec4; a Vec2 and a Vec3 give a Vec4 with the third input's last component dropped. Components are taken in order until there are four.
kg.node.vector_concat.out.out: The concatenation, at most four components wide.
kg.node.vector_concat.option.inputs.tool: How many vectors to join, from 2 to 4.
kg.node.vector_concat.note.1: Four components is the widest vector this graph has, so anything past the fourth is discarded rather than making a wider type.
kg.node.vector_concat.note.2: To add a plain number rather than a vector, use Append Component — a number cannot be wired into a vector pin.
kg.node.vector_append.tooltip: Adds one more component to the end of a vector.
kg.node.vector_append.desc.1: The way to widen a vector with a number: a Vec2 texture coordinate plus a layer, a Vec3 colour plus an alpha. The input keeps its components and the value becomes the new last one.
kg.node.vector_append.in.value: The number to put in the new component.
kg.node.vector_append.out.out: A vector one component wider than the input.
kg.node.vector_append.note.1: A 4-component input comes back unchanged — there is nowhere to append to. Set Component is the node for replacing W.
kg.node.vector_set_component.tooltip: Copies a vector with one component replaced.
kg.node.vector_set_component.desc.1: Changing a single axis without disturbing the others: pinning an entity's Y to the ground while leaving X and Z alone.
kg.node.vector_set_component.in.value: The new value for the chosen component.
kg.node.vector_set_component.out.out: The vector with that component replaced, same width as the input.
kg.node.vector_set_component.option.axis: Which component to replace: 0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z, 3 for W. Defaults to 1, since Y is up in Minecraft.
kg.node.vector_set_component.note.1: An axis outside the input's width leaves the vector unchanged rather than widening it — the same rule Flatten Vector uses.
kg.node.vector_set_component.note.2: Keeps the input's width, which is why this is not Break into Make: that pair would turn a Vec2 or Vec4 into a Vec3 on the way through.
kg.node.vector_get_component.tooltip: One component of a vector, chosen by index.
kg.node.vector_get_component.desc.1: Break Vector is the node for a component you pick while authoring. This is the node for one that is computed — a loop over the three axes, or an axis held in a variable.
kg.node.vector_get_component.in.index: Which component: 0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z, 3 for W.
kg.node.vector_get_component.out.out: That component, or zero if the vector has none.
kg.node.vector_get_component.note.1: An index outside the vector's width reads zero rather than failing, including a negative one.
kg.node.vector_multiply.tooltip: Multiplies two vectors component by component.
kg.node.vector_multiply.desc.1: Scales each axis by a different amount: (a.x*b.x, a.y*b.y, a.z*b.z). This is not the dot product and not the cross product — it is the same shape as adding, with multiplication.
kg.node.vector_multiply.example.1: Damp a velocity horizontally but not vertically: multiply by (0.8, 1, 0.8).
kg.node.vector_multiply.note.1: One factor for every axis is Vector Scale, which is cheaper to read and to wire.
kg.node.vector_multiply.note.2: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_divide.tooltip: Divides two vectors component by component.
kg.node.vector_divide.desc.1: The inverse of Vector Multiply: (a.x/b.x, a.y/b.y, a.z/b.z). Converting between coordinate spaces of different scales, or normalising a position into a box.
kg.node.vector_divide.note.1: A zero divisor gives zero for that component rather than an infinity, exactly as Divide does for numbers. One infinity or NaN entering the graph here would surface far downstream with nothing pointing back.
kg.node.vector_divide.note.2: Because a missing component reads zero, dividing by a narrower vector zeroes the extra components. An unconnected divisor is all zeros, so it answers all zeros.
kg.node.vector_negate.tooltip: Flips a vector to point the opposite way.
kg.node.vector_negate.desc.1: Every component's sign reversed. The length is unchanged; only the direction turns around.
kg.node.vector_negate.out.out: The reversed vector, same width as the input.
kg.node.vector_abs.desc.1: Component-wise magnitude — useful for comparing extents along each axis regardless of direction.
kg.node.vector_abs.in.in: The vector to take the absolute value of.
kg.node.vector_abs.out.out: The vector with every component made positive.
kg.node.vector_abs.note.1: This is not the vector's length. Vector Length is the single number; this is a vector.
kg.node.vector_min.tooltip: The smaller of each pair of components.
kg.node.vector_min.desc.1: Taken with Vector Max, this is how you build the box around two points: Min gives the low corner and Max the high one, whichever way round the inputs came.
kg.node.vector_min.note.1: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_max.tooltip: The larger of each pair of components.
kg.node.vector_max.desc.1: The high corner of the box around two points. See Vector Min for the other one.
kg.node.vector_max.note.1: Works at any width. A Vector pin takes 2, 3 or 4 components and answers in kind: the result is as wide as the wider input, and any component that is not there reads zero.
kg.node.vector_clamp.tooltip: Holds every component between two numbers.
kg.node.vector_clamp.desc.1: Keeps a vector inside a cube: clamping to 0 and 1 for a colour, or to -1 and 1 for a direction fed into something that expects one.
kg.node.vector_clamp.in.min: The lowest any component may be.
kg.node.vector_clamp.in.max: The highest any component may be.
kg.node.vector_clamp.out.out: The clamped vector, same width as the input.
kg.node.vector_clamp.note.1: The bounds are single numbers, applied to every component. For a different range per axis, use Vector Max against the low corner followed by Vector Min against the high one.
kg.node.vector_clamp.note.2: An inverted range — min above max — answers min, the same resolution Clamp reaches for numbers.
kg.node.vector_clamp.note.3: This changes the direction as well as the length. To cap how long a vector is without turning it, use Clamp Length.
kg.node.vector_round.tooltip: Rounds, truncates or takes the sign of every component.
kg.node.vector_round.desc.1: One node for the whole family, because what a graph looks for is 'round a vector' and the flavour is a detail of that. Every mode acts on each component independently and keeps the input's width.
kg.node.vector_round.out.out: The processed vector, same width as the input.
kg.node.vector_round.option.op.tooltip: Which operation to apply to each component.
kg.node.vector_round.option.op.tooltip.R: To the nearest whole number; exact halves go up.
kg.node.vector_round.option.op.tooltip.F: Down to the next whole number. -2.3 becomes -3.
kg.node.vector_round.option.op.tooltip.C: Up to the next whole number. -2.3 becomes -2.
kg.node.vector_round.option.op.tooltip.T: Toward zero, dropping the fraction. -2.7 becomes -2, where Floor would give -3.
kg.node.vector_round.option.op.tooltip.F: Just the fractional part, always from 0 up to but not including 1.
kg.node.vector_round.option.op.tooltip.S: -1, 0 or 1 depending on the component's sign.
kg.node.vector_round.example.1: Floor a position to get the corner of the block containing it. For a BlockPos rather than a vector, Vector To Position already does this.
kg.node.vector_length_squared.tooltip: The vector's length, without the square root.
kg.node.vector_length_squared.desc.1: Squared lengths order the same way real lengths do, so any comparison — nearer, further, within range — can be made on these and skip a square root. Compare against the square of the distance you mean.
kg.node.vector_length_squared.out.out: The sum of the squared components.
kg.node.vector_length_squared.note.1: Only useful for comparing. The number itself is not a distance — a length of 5 reads as 25 here.
kg.node.vector_distance_squared.tooltip: The distance between two points, without the square root.
kg.node.vector_distance_squared.desc.1: Length Squared for the gap between two positions — the cheap form of a range check.
'Is the player within 8 blocks' is this against 64, with no square root anywhere in the graph.
kg.node.vector_clamp_length.tooltip: Holds a vector's length between two numbers, keeping its direction.
kg.node.vector_clamp_length.desc.1: A speed limit that does not steer. Clamping the components instead would cap each axis separately, which turns a diagonal movement as it caps it.
kg.node.vector_clamp_length.in.min: The shortest the result may be.
kg.node.vector_clamp_length.in.max: The longest the result may be.
kg.node.vector_clamp_length.out.out: The vector, rescaled if it was outside the range.
kg.node.vector_clamp_length.note.1: A zero vector stays zero even when the minimum is above zero: it has no direction to stretch along, and inventing one would be a guess.
kg.node.vector_project.tooltip: The part of one vector that lies along another.
kg.node.vector_project.desc.1: Splits a vector into the half that points along a given direction. How much of a velocity is 'forward', how far along a rail a push actually moves something.
kg.node.vector_project.out.out: The part of a lying along b.
kg.node.vector_project.note.1: b does not have to be a unit vector — its length divides out. A zero b names no direction to project onto and answers zero.
kg.node.vector_project.note.2: Project and Reject are the two halves of the same split: added back together they give a exactly.
kg.node.vector_reject.tooltip: The part of one vector that does not lie along another.
kg.node.vector_reject.desc.1: The sideways half of the split Project makes: the part of a movement a wall does not stop, or a velocity with its climb removed.
kg.node.vector_reject.out.out: The part of a perpendicular to b.
kg.node.vector_reject.example.1: Reject a movement against a wall's normal to get the slide along it — the vector that keeps an entity moving instead of stopping dead.
kg.node.vector_reject.note.1: A zero b removes nothing and answers a unchanged.
kg.node.vector_reflect.tooltip: Bounces a direction off a surface.
kg.node.vector_reflect.desc.1: Mirrors the input about the plane the normal describes, so the angle coming in equals the angle going out. A projectile off a wall, a look direction off a mirror.
kg.node.vector_reflect.note.1: The normal is normalised internally, so it does not have to arrive with length 1. A zero normal is no surface at all and passes the input straight through.
kg.node.vector_reflect.note.2: The result keeps the input's length. Reflecting does not slow anything down; multiply afterwards for a lossy bounce.
kg.node.vector_angle_between.tooltip: The angle in degrees between two directions.
kg.node.vector_angle_between.desc.1: Always from 0 to 180, and never says which way to turn. This counts pitch as well as yaw, so it is the answer to 'how far off am I' in three dimensions.
kg.node.vector_angle_between.note.1: Yaw Between is the node for a turn to apply: it is signed, and it ignores the vertical axis.
kg.node.vector_angle_between.note.2: Neither input has to be a unit vector. Either one being zero has no angle to report and answers 0.
kg.node.vector_rotate_axis.tooltip: Turns a vector about an arbitrary axis, by an angle in degrees.
kg.node.vector_rotate_axis.desc.1: The general rotation: any axis, not just X, Y or Z. Right-handed, so a positive angle turns counter-clockwise when seen from the tip of the axis looking back down it — the same handedness as Cross Product.
kg.node.vector_rotate_axis.in.angle: How far to turn, in degrees.
kg.node.vector_rotate_axis.example.1: Rotate a forward direction about world up to sweep a cone of search directions, or about the right vector to aim above a target.
kg.node.vector_rotate_axis.note.1: The axis does not have to be a unit vector — it is normalised internally. A zero axis names no rotation and passes the input through.
kg.node.vector_rotate_axis.note.2: Genuinely three-dimensional, like Cross Product: a 2- or 4-component input is read as its first three and the answer is always a Vec3.
kg.node.vector_from_rotation.tooltip: The unit direction an entity with this yaw and pitch is looking.
kg.node.vector_from_rotation.desc.1: Minecraft's own convention, taken from the game rather than re-derived: yaw 0 looks toward +Z, yaw -90 toward +X, and a positive pitch looks down.
kg.node.vector_from_rotation.in.yaw: Rotation about the vertical axis, in degrees.
kg.node.vector_from_rotation.in.pitch: Rotation up or down, in degrees. Positive looks down.
kg.node.vector_from_rotation.out.out: A unit vector pointing that way.
kg.node.vector_from_rotation.note.1: The result always has length 1, so it can go straight into a dot product or be scaled to a reach.
kg.node.vector_to_rotation.tooltip: The yaw and pitch that would face along this vector.
kg.node.vector_to_rotation.desc.1: The inverse of Direction From Rotation, in the same convention — feed these to anything that sets an entity's rotation.
kg.node.vector_to_rotation.out.yaw: Rotation about the vertical axis, in degrees, from -180 to 180.
kg.node.vector_to_rotation.out.pitch: Rotation up or down, in degrees, from -90 to 90. Positive looks down.
kg.node.vector_to_rotation.note.1: The input does not have to be a unit vector; only its direction matters. A zero vector has no direction and answers zero for both.
kg.node.vector_move_towards.tooltip: A step from one point toward another, no longer than a given distance.
kg.node.vector_move_towards.desc.1: Chasing without overshoot. Once the gap is within one step the result is exactly the target, so the movement settles rather than oscillating around it — which is the difference between this and a Lerp with a small t.
kg.node.vector_move_towards.in.maxDelta: The furthest this step may travel.
kg.node.vector_move_towards.note.1: A negative step moves away from the target instead, at that speed.
kg.node.vector_nearly_equals.tooltip: Whether two vectors agree to within a tolerance.
kg.node.vector_nearly_equals.desc.1: The comparison to reach for instead of testing equality. Two floats that came from different arithmetic are almost never bit-identical, so an exact test on a computed vector reads as correct and is false forever.
kg.node.vector_nearly_equals.in.epsilon: How far apart a component may be and still count as equal.
kg.node.vector_nearly_equals.out.out: True when every component is within the tolerance.
kg.node.vector_nearly_equals.note.1: Compared over the wider input's width, so a Vec4 differing only in W is not reported as equal to a Vec3.
kg.node.vector_nearly_equals.note.2: Compare against a zero vector to ask whether something is standing still or has no direction.
kg.node.mc_id_create.tooltip: Builds a namespaced id from its two halves.
kg.node.mc_id_create.desc.1: An id that cannot be formed — an illegal character in either half — comes out null rather than throwing, because an id assembled from graph data is user input.
kg.node.mc_id_create.in.namespace: The mod or datapack id, usually minecraft.
kg.node.mc_id_create.in.path: The name within that namespace, such as diamond.
kg.node.mc_id_unpack.desc.1: Reading the whole identifier as text needs no node — anything converts to text on a String pin. This is for comparing one half: testing the namespace answers "is this one of mine?" without splitting strings in the graph.
kg.node.mc_id_unpack.out.namespace: The part before the colon — the mod or datapack it belongs to.
kg.node.mc_id_parse.desc.1: A string with no colon takes the minecraft namespace, matching how the game reads ids everywhere else.
kg.node.mc_id_parse.out.out: The parsed id, or nothing when the text is not one.
kg.node.mc_id_parse.out.valid: Whether the text was a well-formed id.
kg.node.mc_item_from_id.tooltip: Looks a item up by id.
kg.node.mc_item_from_id.desc.1: An unknown id yields nothing and reports found = false. That matters here: this registry is defaulted, so asking it directly would hand back air or empty and turn a typo into a legitimate-looking answer.
kg.node.mc_item_from_id.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_item_from_id.out.found: Whether the id named something that exists.
kg.node.mc_block_from_id.tooltip: Looks a block up by id.
kg.node.mc_block_from_id.desc.1: An unknown id yields nothing and reports found = false. That matters here: this registry is defaulted, so asking it directly would hand back air or empty and turn a typo into a legitimate-looking answer.
kg.node.mc_block_from_id.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_block_from_id.out.found: Whether the id named something that exists.
kg.node.mc_fluid_from_id.tooltip: Looks a fluid up by id.
kg.node.mc_fluid_from_id.desc.1: An unknown id yields nothing and reports found = false. That matters here: this registry is defaulted, so asking it directly would hand back air or empty and turn a typo into a legitimate-looking answer.
kg.node.mc_fluid_from_id.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_fluid_from_id.out.found: Whether the id named something that exists.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_from_id.tooltip: Looks a entity type up by id.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_from_id.desc.1: An unknown id yields nothing and reports found = false. That matters here: this registry is defaulted, so asking it directly would hand back air or empty and turn a typo into a legitimate-looking answer.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_from_id.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_from_id.out.found: Whether the id named something that exists.
kg.node.mc_item_id.tooltip: The registry id of a item.
kg.node.mc_item_id.desc.1: The reverse of the lookup node. Useful for comparing against a configured id, or for showing what something is.
kg.node.mc_item_id.out.out: Its id, or nothing if it is not registered.
kg.node.mc_block_id.tooltip: The registry id of a block.
kg.node.mc_block_id.desc.1: The reverse of the lookup node. Useful for comparing against a configured id, or for showing what something is.
kg.node.mc_block_id.out.out: Its id, or nothing if it is not registered.
kg.node.mc_fluid_id.tooltip: The registry id of a fluid.
kg.node.mc_fluid_id.desc.1: The reverse of the lookup node. Useful for comparing against a configured id, or for showing what something is.
kg.node.mc_fluid_id.out.out: Its id, or nothing if it is not registered.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_id.tooltip: The registry id of a entity type.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_id.desc.1: The reverse of the lookup node. Useful for comparing against a configured id, or for showing what something is.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_id.out.out: Its id, or nothing if it is not registered.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_props.tooltip: An entity type's name, hitbox and category.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_props.desc.1: What an entity type is, as opposed to what a live entity is doing — that is what the Entity Info node is for. A type is a registry entry with a handful of static facts; an entity has hundreds of changing ones.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_props.desc.2: Width is the full edge of the square footprint, not a radius, so a player reads 0.6 by 1.8. These are the numbers to build a box from when checking whether an entity would fit somewhere before spawning one.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_props.out.name: The type's display name.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_props.out.width: Full width of the hitbox footprint.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_props.out.fireImm: Whether entities of this type ignore fire.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_props.out.categor: Spawn category — monster, creature, ambient and so on.
kg.node.mc_block_in_tag.tooltip: Whether a block belongs to a tag.
kg.node.mc_block_in_tag.desc.1: Tags live in the blocks folder of a datapack. A tag id that does not exist is false rather than an error, since a tag id is data.
kg.node.mc_block_in_tag.in.tag: The tag's id, such as minecraft:planks.
kg.node.mc_block_in_tag.out.out: Whether it is in the tag.
kg.node.mc_fluid_in_tag.tooltip: Whether a fluid belongs to a tag.
kg.node.mc_fluid_in_tag.desc.1: Tags live in the fluids folder of a datapack. A tag id that does not exist is false rather than an error, since a tag id is data.
kg.node.mc_fluid_in_tag.in.tag: The tag's id, such as minecraft:planks.
kg.node.mc_fluid_in_tag.out.out: Whether it is in the tag.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_in_tag.tooltip: Whether a entity type belongs to a tag.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_in_tag.desc.1: Tags live in the entity_types folder of a datapack. A tag id that does not exist is false rather than an error, since a tag id is data.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_in_tag.in.tag: The tag's id, such as minecraft:planks.
kg.node.mc_entity_type_in_tag.out.out: Whether it is in the tag.
kg.node.mc_items_in_tag.desc.1: Lists the contents of an item tag. Membership answers whether one item is in a tag; this answers what is in it, which no command can.
kg.node.mc_items_in_tag.note.1: Order follows the tag files, nested tags flattened in place. It is stable for a fixed set of packs but is not alphabetical, so sort by id when the choice has to be reproducible.
kg.node.mc_items_in_tag.out.found: False when no pack defines this tag. The list is empty either way, so this is what tells the two apart.
kg.node.mc_blocks_in_tag.desc.1: Lists the contents of a block tag — every log, every ore, everything a pickaxe can mine. Useful for a graph that has to act on a whole family of blocks rather than test one.
kg.node.mc_blocks_in_tag.note.1: Order follows the tag files, nested tags flattened in place. It is stable for a fixed set of packs but is not alphabetical, so sort by id when the choice has to be reproducible.
kg.node.mc_blocks_in_tag.out.found: False when no pack defines this tag. The list is empty either way, so this is what tells the two apart.
kg.node.mc_entity_types_in_tag.tooltip: Every entity type a tag contains.
kg.node.mc_entity_types_in_tag.desc.1: Lists the contents of an entity-type tag, e.g. every skeleton or everything that can be frozen. A spawner graph reads one of these instead of naming mobs one at a time.
kg.node.mc_entity_types_in_tag.note.1: Order follows the tag files, nested tags flattened in place. It is stable for a fixed set of packs but is not alphabetical, so sort by id when the choice has to be reproducible.
kg.node.mc_entity_types_in_tag.out.out: The entity types in the tag.
kg.node.mc_entity_types_in_tag.out.found: False when no pack defines this tag. The list is empty either way, so this is what tells the two apart.
kg.node.mc_fluids_in_tag.desc.1: Lists the contents of a fluid tag. Small tags, mostly: minecraft:water holds the still and flowing forms, which is exactly the pair a graph keeps forgetting about.
kg.node.mc_fluids_in_tag.note.1: Order follows the tag files, nested tags flattened in place. It is stable for a fixed set of packs but is not alphabetical, so sort by id when the choice has to be reproducible.
kg.node.mc_fluids_in_tag.out.found: False when no pack defines this tag. The list is empty either way, so this is what tells the two apart.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_in_tag.tooltip: Whether a stack belongs to a tag.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_in_tag.desc.1: Tags live in the items folder of a datapack. A tag id that does not exist is false rather than an error, since a tag id is data.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_in_tag.in.tag: The tag's id, such as minecraft:planks.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_in_tag.out.out: Whether it is in the tag.
kg.node.mc_block_state_in_tag.tooltip: Whether a state belongs to a tag.
kg.node.mc_block_state_in_tag.desc.1: Tags live in the blocks folder of a datapack. A tag id that does not exist is false rather than an error, since a tag id is data.
kg.node.mc_block_state_in_tag.in.tag: The tag's id, such as minecraft:planks.
kg.node.mc_block_state_in_tag.out.out: Whether it is in the tag.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_add.tooltip: Adds two block positions component by component.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_add.desc.1: Adding a position to an offset moves it; the second input is usually the offset rather than a place.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_subtract.tooltip: Subtracts one block position from another.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_subtract.desc.1: Subtracting positions gives the offset between them, which is what to feed a direction test or a distance.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_distance.tooltip: How far apart two block positions are.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_distance.desc.1: Both forms are given because the squared one is the one to compare against a squared radius — a range check needs no square root, and the game's own code avoids it for the same reason.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_distance.out.sqr: The distance squared, with no square root taken.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_to_vector.tooltip: A block position as a vector.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_to_vector.desc.1: A block position names a block, not a point, so there are two defensible answers. The centre is what entity positions and rays want; the corner is what a grid calculation wants.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_to_vector.in.center: On for the middle of the block, off for its lowest corner. On by default, which is what positions and rays expect.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_unpack.desc.1: The inverse of Block Pos Create. Three integers, not a vector, because a block position is an integer triple — reading a coordinate through Block Pos To Vector would round-trip it through floating point for no reason.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_from_vector.desc.1: Floors rather than rounds — the same rule the game uses to decide which block an entity stands in. Rounding would put the boundary in the middle of a block.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_between.tooltip: Every block position in the box between two corners.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_between.desc.1: Inclusive of both corners. The list is capped, and truncated says whether it was — an unbounded box is millions of entries, which would stall a tick before it ran out of memory.
kg.node.mc_block_pos_between.out.truncat: Whether the list stopped short of covering the whole box.
kg.node.mc_aabb_from_corners.desc.1: The corners may be given in either order; the box normalises them.
kg.node.mc_aabb_from_block_pos.tooltip: The one-block cube a position names.
kg.node.mc_aabb_from_block_pos.desc.1: The box from the block's corner to one block along each axis — what a block occupies.
kg.node.mc_aabb_around.tooltip: A cube centred on a point.
kg.node.mc_aabb_around.desc.1: Size is the full edge length rather than a radius, so a size of 2 around the origin spans -1 to 1.
kg.node.mc_aabb_inflate.tooltip: Grows a box on every side.
kg.node.mc_aabb_inflate.desc.1: A negative amount shrinks it. Growing by the reach distance is how a range check becomes a box test.
kg.node.mc_aabb_inflate.in.amount: How far to grow each side.
kg.node.mc_aabb_union.tooltip: The smallest box containing both inputs.
kg.node.mc_aabb_union.desc.1: Not the overlapping part — that is Intersect. This grows to cover both.
kg.node.mc_aabb_intersect.tooltip: The overlapping part of two boxes.
kg.node.mc_aabb_intersect.desc.1: Undefined when they do not overlap — the result can have inverted edges. Test with Boxes Intersect first.
kg.node.mc_aabb_intersects.tooltip: Whether two boxes overlap at all.
kg.node.mc_aabb_intersects.desc.1: The test to run before taking an intersection, and the cheap way to ask whether two things could be touching.
kg.node.mc_aabb_contains.tooltip: Whether a point is inside a box.
kg.node.mc_aabb_contains.desc.1: The maximum edges are exclusive, as everywhere in the game — a point exactly on the far face is outside.
kg.node.mc_aabb_unpack.desc.1: Outputs are double-precision because a box is: these are world coordinates, and a float cannot represent a half-block offset once you are a few million blocks from the origin. Nothing forces this node through the vector type, so it does not pay that precision cost.
kg.node.mc_aabb_center.tooltip: A bounding box's centre point and its size along each axis.
kg.node.mc_aabb_center.desc.1: The centre comes out as the graph's vector type. That is the whole reason this is a node: Minecraft's own getter returns a Vec3, which the graph deliberately does not carry, so the value has to be converted at the boundary.
kg.node.mc_aabb_center.desc.2: Sizes are the full edge lengths, not half-extents.
kg.node.mc_aabb_center.out.center: The point at the middle of the box.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_create.desc.1: Chunk coordinates count chunks, not blocks — chunk 1 starts at block 16.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_from_block_pos.tool: Which chunk a block position falls in.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_from_block_pos.desc: Divides by 16 the way the game does, which is a shift — so it is correct on the negative side, where a plain division is not.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_origin.desc.1: At y = 0. The origin every chunk-relative calculation counts from.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_unpack.tooltip: A chunk's coordinates and the block range it covers.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_unpack.desc.1: The block bounds are here rather than in a node of their own because they are what a chunk coordinate is usually wanted for — iterating a chunk's blocks needs all four, and working them out by hand is exactly the 16-block shift arithmetic this group exists to keep out of graphs.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_unpack.out.x: Chunk X — block X divided by 16.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_unpack.out.minBlock: East-west coordinate of the chunk's first block.
North-south coordinate of the chunk's first block.
kg.node.mc_chunk_pos_unpack.out.maxBlock: East-west coordinate of the chunk's last block, inclusive.
North-south coordinate of the chunk's last block, inclusive.
kg.node.mc_direction_rotate.tooltip: Applies a block rotation to a direction.
kg.node.mc_direction_rotate.desc.1: The same transform a structure block applies, so a graph placing rotated structures can rotate its directions to match.
kg.node.mc_direction_mirror.tooltip: Reflects a direction across a plane.
kg.node.mc_direction_mirror.desc.1: Left-right flips north and south; front-back flips east and west. Which is which is easy to get backwards.
kg.node.mc_direction_turn.tooltip: A quarter turn about an axis.
kg.node.mc_direction_turn.desc.1: One node for both ways round, so a graph can choose at runtime. About the Y axis this is the ordinary left/right turn.
kg.node.mc_direction_turn.in.clockwise: On to turn clockwise, off for anticlockwise.
kg.node.mc_direction_turn.in.axis: The axis to turn about. Y is the usual one — a turn about Y is a left or right turn.
kg.node.mc_direction_normal.tooltip: The direction's unit offset, as three whole numbers.
kg.node.mc_direction_normal.desc.1: Three numbers rather than a vector, because this is an offset rather than a position — feed them into Make Vector or Make Chunk Pos as needed. Note that north is negative Z.
kg.node.mc_direction_data.tooltip: A direction's rotation angle and its two index encodings.
kg.node.mc_direction_data.desc.1: The rotation is the reason this node exists: it is the one direction property that is arithmetic rather than a lookup, and it is what a model or an entity needs to be turned to face this way.
kg.node.mc_direction_data.desc.2: The two indices are the game's own packings. Use them to index an array by direction.
kg.node.mc_direction_data.out.yRot: Degrees to rotate about the vertical axis to face this way.
kg.node.mc_direction_data.out.data2D: Index among the four horizontal faces, or -1 for up and down.
kg.node.mc_direction_from_name.tooltip: Parses a direction name such as north.
kg.node.mc_direction_from_name.desc.1: An unrecognised name falls back to north and reports found = false, so a graph can tell a typo from a genuine north.
kg.node.mc_direction_from_name.in.name: The name to parse.
kg.node.mc_direction_nearest.tooltip: The face a vector points most nearly along.
kg.node.mc_direction_nearest.desc.1: How to turn an arbitrary heading — a look vector, an offset between two positions — into one of the six faces.
kg.node.mc_direction_all.tooltip: The directions, as a list to iterate.
kg.node.mc_direction_all.desc.1: Feed it into For Each to look at every neighbour of a block.
kg.node.mc_direction_all.option.plane.to: Horizontal gives the four compass directions, vertical gives up and down. Horizontal is the default, since anything walking on the ground wants those four.
kg.node.mc_block_default_state.desc.1: The bridge from a block to a block state — the form world queries and property nodes work with.
kg.node.mc_block_state_block.tooltip: The block a state belongs to.
kg.node.mc_block_state_block.desc.1: The way back from Block State to Block, and the counterpart of Block Default State. A state carries a block plus its property values; this drops the properties.
kg.node.mc_block_state_block.out.out: The block. Air if no state was given.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.tooltip: A block state's physical properties, in one node.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.desc.1: Seven facts and a light level together rather than eight nodes, because they are never wanted alone — anything walking a region asks several of these about every state it sees, and a node per flag would mean seven wires leaving the same state.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.desc.2: Is Air is the one that carries most of the weight: it is how a graph tests whether there is anything at a position, given a state it already has.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.out.air: True for air and its variants — nothing is there.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.out.solid: Whether the state forms a solid body.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.out.liquid: Whether the state is a fluid.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.out.canOccl: Whether it blocks light and hides neighbouring faces.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.out.hasBloc: Whether it carries a block entity, and so may hold data.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.out.randoml: Whether the game ticks it at random — crops, leaves, ice.
kg.node.mc_block_state_flags.out.lightEm: How much light it gives off, 0 to 15.
kg.node.mc_block_props.desc.1: These belong to the block type rather than to any one state. The movement factors are what makes ice slippery and soul sand slow; resistance and destroy time are what a graph implementing mining or blast logic compares against.
kg.node.mc_block_props.out.name: The block's display name.
kg.node.mc_block_props.out.friction: Surface friction. Above the default 0.6 is slippery.
kg.node.mc_block_props.out.speedFactor: Multiplier applied to the speed of entities on it.
kg.node.mc_block_props.out.jumpFactor: Multiplier applied to the jump height of entities on it.
kg.node.mc_block_props.out.destroyTime: Base hardness — how long it takes to break.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.tooltip: How hard the block at a position is, and roughly how long it takes to break.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.desc.1: What a mining graph needs to decide whether a block is worth the time. No command answers it.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.note.1: With a player wired, this asks the game directly, so the answer includes that player's held tool, its Efficiency, Haste and Mining Fatigue, being underwater and being off the ground. The tool input is ignored in that case, because the player's own held item is what the game uses.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.note.2: Without a player it falls back to hardness against the tool's speed, which is the same formula minus every modifier above. Good enough to compare two blocks or plan a machine, but not the number a particular player will see. Exact says which of the two you got.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.note.3: Ticks is -1 for a block that cannot be broken at all, so a graph sorting by time does not put bedrock first. Unbreakable is the flag to branch on.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.in.tool: What it would be broken with. Ignored when a player is given.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.in.player: Whose mining speed to use. Leave empty for a tool-only estimate.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.out.hardness: The block's hardness at that position. -1 means it never breaks.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.out.progress: How much of the block is broken per tick.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.out.ticks: How long it takes, in ticks, or -1 for never.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.out.unbreakable: True when it cannot be broken at all.
kg.node.mc_destroy_speed.out.exact: True when a player was given, so the answer is the real one rather than an estimate.
kg.node.mc_can_harvest.tooltip: Whether breaking a block with a tool will actually drop anything.
kg.node.mc_can_harvest.desc.1: Stone with a hand still breaks, it just gives nothing back. That gap is what this answers, and it is the check a mining graph makes before spending the time.
kg.node.mc_can_harvest.note.1: Requires Tool is the block's own rule, kept separate from the verdict: "yes, and anything works" and "yes, because you happen to be holding the right thing" lead to different decisions when the tool might change.
kg.node.mc_can_harvest.note.2: No world input, because this is a property of the state and the item rather than of a position. Enchantments do not enter into it either — Silk Touch changes what drops, not whether anything does.
kg.node.mc_can_harvest.in.tool: What it would be broken with. An empty stack means bare hands.
kg.node.mc_can_harvest.out.requiresTool: Whether the block insists on a particular tool at all.
kg.node.mc_block_state_properties.toolti: Every property name a state carries.
kg.node.mc_block_state_properties.desc.1: For discovering what a state can be asked about, rather than guessing property names.
kg.node.mc_block_state_get_property.tool: Reads one block-state property as text.
kg.node.mc_block_state_get_property.desc: Values are the same text that appears in a command or the F3 screen, because a property's Java type depends on which property it is and a port cannot follow that.
kg.node.mc_block_state_get_property.in.n: The property's name, such as facing.
Whether the state has that property.
kg.node.mc_block_state_set_property.tool: Writes one block-state property from text.
kg.node.mc_block_state_set_property.desc: An unknown property or an illegal value reports ok = false and passes the state through unchanged, so one bad edit does not poison a chain of them.
kg.node.mc_block_state_set_property.in.v: The value to set, as text.
Whether the property existed and the value was legal.
kg.node.mc_block_state_is_block.tooltip: Whether a state belongs to a block.
kg.node.mc_block_state_is_block.desc.1: Compares the block and ignores every property, which is usually the question — any stair is a stair.
kg.node.mc_block_state_rotate.tooltip: The state as it would appear rotated.
kg.node.mc_block_state_rotate.desc.1: Rotates the properties that follow rotation — a stair's facing, a log's axis — and leaves the rest alone.
kg.node.mc_block_state_mirror.tooltip: The state as it would appear mirrored.
kg.node.mc_block_state_mirror.desc.1: Reflects the direction-dependent properties across the chosen plane.
kg.node.mc_block_state_fluid.tooltip: The fluid a state is, or contains.
kg.node.mc_block_state_fluid.desc.1: Water for a water block and also for a waterlogged stair — this asks what fluid is in the state, not whether the block is one.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_with_count.tooltip: The same stack with a different count.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_with_count.desc.1: Returns a copy; the input is untouched. A count of zero or less gives an empty stack.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_unpack.tooltip: What an item stack is: its item, how many, and whether it is nothing.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_unpack.desc.1: The three fundamentals, and the inverse of Item Stack Create.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_unpack.desc.2: Is Empty is its own output rather than something to infer from a count of zero, because the game's own emptiness test also covers a stack holding air.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_unpack.out.count: How many are in the stack.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_unpack.out.empty: True when the stack holds nothing.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_damage.desc.1: Damage counts up from zero the way the game stores it: a fresh tool reads 0 and a nearly-broken one approaches its maximum. To show remaining durability, subtract.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_damage.note.1: Is Damageable is separate from Is Damaged for a reason. A stone block reports damage 0 and max damage 0, and dividing those is how a not-a-number ends up in a tooltip — check Is Damageable first.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_damage.out.damage: Damage taken so far, counting up from zero.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_damage.out.maxDama: Damage at which the item breaks. Zero for items that cannot be damaged.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_damage.out.damaged: True when damage has been taken.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_damage.out.damagea: True when the item can be damaged at all.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.tooltip: A copy of the stack with its durability set.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.desc.1: The write half of Item Damage, counted the same way: damage is wear, so 0 is a fresh tool and the maximum is one about to break. A graph thinking in remaining durability has to subtract.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.note.1: Out of range is clamped rather than refused, which is the game's own behaviour and keeps a subtraction that went negative from failing the node.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.note.2: An item with no durability — a diamond, a block — is refused and passes through unchanged. It is not that the write failed; there is nothing there to write to.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.note.3: At exactly the maximum the item still exists. The game destroys a tool on the use after that, not here, so Broken means "one more use" rather than "gone".
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.in.stac: The stack to base the copy on.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.in.dama: How worn the copy should be, in points of damage.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.out.bro: True when the copy is at its maximum damage.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_damage.out.ok: False for an empty stack or an item with no durability.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_limits.tooltip: How large a stack may get, and whether it is enchanted.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_limits.desc.1: The maximum is this stack's own, which a data component can raise or lower away from the item's default — Item Properties gives the default instead.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_limits.out.maxStac: The largest count this stack may hold.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_limits.out.stackab: Whether more than one fits in a slot.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_limits.out.enchant: Whether the stack carries any enchantment.
kg.node.mc_item_props.tooltip: An item type's own constants, independent of any stack.
kg.node.mc_item_props.desc.1: For asking about an item you have without inventing a stack to hold it. The stack size here is the item's default; a particular stack's limit can differ, and Item Stack Limits is where to read that.
kg.node.mc_item_props.out.name: The item's display name.
kg.node.mc_item_props.out.enchantmentVal: How receptive the item is to enchanting — higher gives better results.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_same_item.tooltip: Whether two stacks hold the same item.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_same_item.desc.1: Ignores count and components — the question is is this a diamond, not is this the same diamond sword.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_same_components.de: Same item and same components, which is the test that decides whether two stacks would merge in an inventory. Count is still ignored.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_display_name.toolt: The name shown in a tooltip.
The custom name if the stack has one, otherwise the item's own name.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_custom_data.toolti: The stack's custom data as NBT.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_custom_data.desc.1: This is where arbitrary mod data lives — the typed replacement for the whole-stack tag older versions had. A stack with none reads as an empty compound, so a graph can always ask a question of the result.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_custom_data.out.ou: A copy of the custom data.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_custom_data.to: Stores custom data on a copy of the stack.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_custom_data.de: Returns a new stack; the input is untouched, which matters because a pull-evaluated graph may hand the same stack to several branches.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_custom_name.toolti: The stack's custom name, if it was renamed.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_custom_name.desc.1: has distinguishes a renamed stack from one showing its default name, which the name alone cannot.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_custom_name.out.ou: The custom name, or empty text.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_custom_name.out.ha: Whether a custom name was set.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_custom_name.to: Renames a copy of the stack.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_set_custom_name.de: An empty name input removes the custom name rather than setting a blank one, so this node can also undo a rename.
kg.node.mc_item_stack_lore.desc.1: The extra tooltip lines below the name. Empty when the stack has none.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_create.desc.1: Amounts are in millibuckets, where a bucket is 1000. An empty fluid or a zero amount both give an empty stack.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_with_amount.toolt: The same fluid in a different amount.
Returns a copy; the input is untouched.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_unpack.tooltip: What a fluid stack is: which fluid, how much, and whether it is nothing.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_unpack.desc.1: Amounts are in millibuckets, where a bucket is 1000.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_unpack.desc.2: Is Empty is its own output because an empty stack and a stack with a zero amount are both empty, and only the game's own predicate covers both.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_unpack.out.empty: True when the stack holds nothing.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_unpack.out.name: The fluid's display name.
kg.node.mc_fluid_bucket.tooltip: The bucket item that holds a fluid.
kg.node.mc_fluid_bucket.desc.1: The only property of a fluid itself worth a node — a fluid's other readable values are its state definition and its fluid type, neither of which the graph carries. A fluid with no bucket form gives air.
kg.node.mc_fluid_bucket.out.out: The filled bucket item, or air if the fluid has none.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_same_fluid.toolti: Whether two stacks hold the same fluid.
kg.node.mc_fluid_stack_same_fluid.desc.1: Ignores the amount, the same way Same Item ignores the count.
kg.node.mc_fluid_to_block.tooltip: The block a fluid forms in the world.
kg.node.mc_fluid_to_block.desc.1: A fluid with no placeable form gives air.
kg.node.mc_fluid_from_block.tooltip: The fluid a block is, or contains.
kg.node.mc_fluid_from_block.desc.1: Goes through the block's default state, so a waterloggable block reports water only if its default state is waterlogged.
kg.node.mc_text_literal.desc.1: No translation happens, so this is for text that is already in the right language — a number, a name, a debug line.
kg.node.mc_text_translatable.tooltip: Text looked up in the reader's language.
kg.node.mc_text_translatable.desc.1: Translation happens on the client, so this is what to use for anything a player reads. A component passed as an argument keeps its own formatting.
kg.node.mc_text_translatable.in.args: Values to substitute into the text.
kg.node.mc_text_append.desc.1: Each half keeps its own formatting, which is what makes this different from joining two strings.
kg.node.mc_text_to_string.tooltip: A component's text, with formatting resolved.
kg.node.mc_text_to_string.desc.1: The one conversion the graph cannot do implicitly: wiring a component to a string pin would use its debug form, not its text. On a server a translation key resolves against the server's language.
kg.node.mc_text_styled.tooltip: Applies a colour and the bold, italic and underline styles.
kg.node.mc_text_styled.desc.1: The colour is an ARGB integer so it can come from anywhere a colour does; only the RGB part is used. Leave it at -1 to keep whatever colour the component already has.
kg.node.mc_text_styled.in.color: The colour, or -1 to leave it alone.
kg.node.mc_text_colored.tooltip: Applies one of the game's named colours.
kg.node.mc_text_colored.desc.1: The simpler alternative to an ARGB integer for the common case where one of the sixteen chat colours will do.
kg.node.mc_get_biome_id.tooltip: The biome at a position, as its id.
kg.node.mc_get_biome_id.desc.1: An id rather than a biome value, because biomes come from datapacks — the set depends on the world, so there is no fixed list to resolve against.
kg.node.mc_get_biome_id.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_get_fluid_state.desc.1: Water for a water block and also for anything waterlogged.
kg.node.mc_get_fluid_state.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_get_light.tooltip: Block light and sky light at a position.
kg.node.mc_get_light.desc.1: Each is 0 to 15. Block light comes from torches and the like; sky light is what reaches the position from above, before the time of day is applied.
kg.node.mc_get_light.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_get_height.tooltip: The surface height of a column.
kg.node.mc_get_height.desc.1: Which heightmap matters: motion blocking stops at the first block that would catch a falling entity, which is the one to use for where would something land.
kg.node.mc_get_height.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_get_height.option.heightmap.t: Which surface to measure to. Motion blocking is the one that answers where something would land; world surface includes leaves and other things you can fall through.
kg.node.mc_can_see_sky.tooltip: Whether a position has open sky above it.
kg.node.mc_can_see_sky.desc.1: What decides whether rain and snow reach a place, and whether the sky lights it.
kg.node.mc_can_see_sky.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_can_see_sky.out.out: Whether the sky is open above.
kg.node.mc_dimension_id.desc.1: minecraft:overworld, minecraft:the_nether and so on — how a graph tells which world it is running in.
kg.node.mc_dimension_id.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_raycast_block.tooltip: Casts a ray and reports the first block it hits.
kg.node.mc_raycast_block.desc.1: Returns the pieces rather than a hit object: the block, the face it entered through, and the exact point. Note that the endpoints are graph vectors, so a ray very far from the origin loses sub-block precision.
kg.node.mc_raycast_block.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_raycast_entity.tooltip: The first entity a ray passes through.
kg.node.mc_raycast_entity.desc.1: The counterpart of Raycast Block, and together with it the answer to "what is this player looking at" — cast both along the look direction and take whichever hit is nearer. They are separate nodes because the game's own hit detection is: blocks are traced through collision shapes, entities through bounding boxes.
kg.node.mc_raycast_entity.note.1: A ray cast from an entity's own eyes starts inside that entity's hitbox, so without excluding it the first thing hit is always itself. Wiring the looking entity into Ignore is almost always what you want.
kg.node.mc_raycast_entity.in.ignore: An entity the ray passes through, usually the one looking.
kg.node.mc_raycast_entity.out.hit: True when an entity was found.
kg.node.mc_raycast_entity.out.point: Where on it the ray landed.
kg.node.mc_entities_in_box.tooltip: Every entity inside a bounding box.
kg.node.mc_entities_in_box.desc.1: The box-typed form, which is what to reach for now — the older two-corner node predates the box type and is kept only so saved graphs stay valid.
kg.node.mc_entities_in_box.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_entities_of_type_in_box.toolt: Every entity of one type inside a box.
Filtering by type in the query is cheaper than fetching everything and filtering afterwards.
kg.node.mc_entities_of_type_in_box.in.le: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_nearest_player.tooltip: The closest player within a radius.
kg.node.mc_nearest_player.desc.1: Creative-mode players are included. found distinguishes nobody nearby from a null that slipped through.
kg.node.mc_nearest_player.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_nearest_player.in.radius: How far to search, in blocks.
kg.node.mc_nearest_player.out.found: Whether a player was within range.
kg.node.mc_is_chunk_loaded.tooltip: Whether a position can be read right now.
kg.node.mc_is_chunk_loaded.desc.1: Every other world query returns a neutral answer for an unloaded chunk — air, light zero, no entities — which is indistinguishable from a real one. This is the node that tells the difference, and a graph scanning far-off positions should check it before believing what it read.
kg.node.mc_is_chunk_loaded.note.1: Deliberately does not load the chunk. Asking a question must not change the world, and a graph sweeping a region would otherwise drag the whole thing into memory a block at a time.
kg.node.mc_is_chunk_loaded.note.2: In Bounds separates the two ways this can be false. Above the build height or past the world's edge there is nothing to load and never will be, so both are false and the answer is "look somewhere else". In bounds but not loaded means "try again later".
kg.node.mc_is_chunk_loaded.out.out: Whether the position can be read right now.
kg.node.mc_is_chunk_loaded.out.inBounds: Whether the position exists in the world at all.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.tooltip: The nearest structure of a given kind, as a position.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.desc.1: /locate answers in chat. Run Command would hand the graph that sentence and leave it to pull three numbers back out of prose that is translated per language. This returns the position.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.note.1: This is the most expensive node in the mod, and unusually so. The search walks candidate chunk positions outward and asks the world generator about each — the same work /locate does, on the server thread, and a wide radius on a slow generator is measured in seconds. Call it in response to something a player did, not on a tick.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.note.2: Radius is in chunks, not blocks, matching the command. It is capped rather than trusted, so a radius wired from a runaway counter cannot search the world.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.note.3: Server side only, and not found when the world was generated with structures turned off.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.in.level: The world to search. Must be a server world.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.in.radius: How far to search, in chunks.
kg.node.mc_find_structure.out.distance: How far away it is, in blocks.
kg.node.mc_entity_is_type.tooltip: Whether an entity is of a given type.
kg.node.mc_entity_is_type.desc.1: An exact type match, not a category — a zombie is not a skeleton even though both are undead. Use a tag test for categories.
kg.node.mc_entity_held_item.tooltip: What the entity holds or wears in one slot.
kg.node.mc_entity_held_item.desc.1: Equipment is a living-entity idea, so anything else — a dropped item, a minecart — has nothing in any slot rather than being an error.
kg.node.mc_entity_held_item.in.slot: Which slot to read — a hand or an armour slot.
kg.node.mc_entity_has_effect.tooltip: Whether a status effect is active, and how strong.
kg.node.mc_entity_has_effect.desc.1: The amplifier is zero-based the way the game counts it: Strength II is amplifier 1. Both numbers read zero when the effect is absent, which has disambiguates.
kg.node.mc_entity_attribute.tooltip: An attribute's current value, after every modifier.
kg.node.mc_entity_attribute.desc.1: found is false both for an unknown id and for an entity that simply does not have that attribute — an arrow has none.
kg.node.mc_entity_attribute.out.found: Whether the entity has that attribute.
kg.node.mc_entity_tags.tooltip: The scoreboard tags on an entity, the ones /tag adds.
kg.node.mc_entity_tags.desc.1: The read half of a pair that was previously half open: the game has /tag add, but /tag list answers in chat, so a graph could write tags and never see them. These are the closest thing an entity has to a free-form flag, which makes them how a blueprint marks an entity as its own.
kg.node.mc_entity_tags.note.1: Nothing to do with the entity-type tags that Entity Type In Tag asks about. Those are datapack groupings of kinds of entity; these are labels on one individual.
kg.node.mc_entity_tags.note.2: Sorted, because the game keeps them in a hash set and a graph reading the first one would otherwise get a different tag on a different launch.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.tooltip: What a villager or wandering trader is offering.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.desc.1: No command reads trades. /data get entity produces the raw offer NBT, which a graph would then have to walk item by item; this hands back the stacks.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.note.1: Four parallel lists, same shape as All Enchantments: same length, same order. Cost B is empty for a trade that only takes one thing.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.note.2: Cost A is the current price, not the listed one, so it already includes demand, the Hero of the Village discount and any reputation adjustment — what a player would pay right now rather than what the trade was created with.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.note.3: Reading a villager's offers is what makes it generate them if it has not yet, so the first read is not quite free and does change the entity. That is the game's own design.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.in.entity: The villager or trader to read.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.out.costB: The second item each trade takes, empty when there is none.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.out.outOfStoc: Whether each trade has been used up for today.
kg.node.mc_villager_trades.out.found: False when the entity does not trade at all.
kg.node.mc_effect_exists.tooltip: Whether a status-effect id is real.
kg.node.mc_effect_exists.desc.1: For validating an id from a config or a variable before using it, and for showing the effect's name.
