kg.node.mc_effect_exists.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_effect_exists.out.displayName: Its name, for showing to a player.
kg.node.mc_sound_exists.tooltip: Whether a sound id is real.
kg.node.mc_sound_exists.desc.1: Validation only — playing a sound is a side effect and belongs to the exec-flow nodes.
kg.node.mc_sound_exists.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_particle_exists.tooltip: Whether a particle id is real.
kg.node.mc_particle_exists.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_attribute_exists.tooltip: Whether an attribute id is real, and its base value.
kg.node.mc_attribute_exists.desc.1: The base value is the attribute's own default, before any entity or modifier is involved.
kg.node.mc_attribute_exists.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_exists.tooltip: Whether an enchantment id is real in this world.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_exists.desc.1: Takes a world because enchantments come from datapacks — the set depends on which packs are loaded, so there is nothing to check against without one.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_exists.in.level: The world to read. Feed it from a graph variable — the executor never holds one itself.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_exists.in.id: The namespaced id to look up.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_exists.out.maxLev: The highest level it can have.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_level.tooltip: The level of one enchantment on a stack.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_level.desc.1: Zero means absent, which is also what Has says — the pair exists because a graph that branches reads Has and one that computes reads Level, and neither should have to convert.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_level.note.1: This needs a world. Enchantments became a datapack registry in 1.21, so an enchantment id only exists relative to a loaded world and cannot be resolved from a static table the way an item or a block can.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_level.in.enchantm: The enchantment's identifier, such as minecraft:sharpness.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_level.in.level: The world, for resolving the identifier.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_level.out.has: True when the stack carries it.
kg.node.mc_enchantment_level.out.found: False when no such enchantment is defined.
kg.node.mc_enchantments.tooltip: Every enchantment on a stack, with its level.
kg.node.mc_enchantments.desc.1: Two parallel lists rather than a map, because the graph's Map keys by value while a list pair survives a For Each with an index — which is how a graph walks them. The lists are the same length and the same order.
kg.node.mc_enchantments.note.1: Alone among the enchantment nodes this needs no world: each entry already knows its own identifier, so nothing has to be looked up.
kg.node.mc_enchantments.out.levels: Their levels, in the same order.
kg.node.mc_potion_effects.tooltip: Every effect a potion stack would apply.
kg.node.mc_potion_effects.desc.1: The base potion's effects followed by any custom ones, so this is what drinking it actually does rather than the two halves read separately.
kg.node.mc_potion_effects.note.1: Three parallel lists rather than a map, same as All Enchantments: same length, same order, which is what survives a For Each with an index.
kg.node.mc_potion_effects.note.2: A duration of -1 means infinite. That is the game's own encoding, so it is passed through rather than clamped to a positive number.
kg.node.mc_potion_effects.note.3: A stack with no potion component reads as zero effects rather than failing.
kg.node.mc_potion_effects.out.amplifiers: Amplifiers, same order. 0 is level I.
kg.node.mc_potion_type.tooltip: The base potion a stack is brewed from.
kg.node.mc_potion_type.desc.1: The named potion on the stack, e.g. minecraft:long_swiftness. Custom effects added on top do not change it.
kg.node.mc_potion_type.note.1: Not found for a stack with no potion component, and equally for one carrying only custom effects — there is no named potion in either case. The effects are on Potion Effects regardless.
kg.node.mc_potion_type.out.found: Whether the stack names a base potion at all.
kg.node.mc_make_potion.tooltip: A single stack of a named potion.
kg.node.mc_make_potion.desc.1: There is no "swiftness potion" item — there is a bottle carrying a potion component. Which item receives it chooses the form: bottle, splash, lingering, or tipped arrow.
kg.node.mc_make_potion.note.1: No check that the item is potion-shaped, matching what /give allows: the game will happily hand you a potion-flavoured stick.
kg.node.mc_make_potion.note.2: An unknown potion id gives an empty stack rather than a plain bottle of water, which would be a plausible-looking wrong answer.
kg.node.mc_make_potion.in.item: Which form to make. Defaults to the drinkable bottle.
kg.node.mc_make_potion.out.ok: False when the potion id is unknown.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.tooltip: A copy of the stack with one more effect on its potion component.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.desc.1: Custom effects stack on top of the base potion instead of replacing it, so this builds potions no brewing stand can make. Applied to a stack with no potion component, it gives it one holding only this effect.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.note.1: A data node: it returns a new stack and writes nothing. Nothing reaches the world until that stack is put somewhere.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.note.2: A duration of -1 means infinite and is accepted. 0 is refused, since an effect that lasts no time is a mistake rather than a request.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.in.stack: The stack to base the copy on.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.in.duration: How long, in ticks. 20 ticks is a second; -1 is infinite.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.in.amplifie: 0 is level I, 1 is level II, and so on.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.out.out: A copy carrying the extra effect.
kg.node.mc_add_custom_effect.out.ok: False for an empty stack, an unknown effect id, or a zero duration.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.tooltip: What a grid of items would craft into.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.desc.1: Asks the game what a crafting table would make of the items you hand it. There is no command that answers this, which is why a blueprint automating a workbench needs a node for it.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.note.1: Width and height are the shape the items sit in, read row by row from the top left. They matter: four planks in a square are a crafting table, the same four in a line are nothing.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.note.2: A list shorter than the grid is padded with empty slots rather than refused, so a list still being assembled is an ordinary state and not an error.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.note.3: The result is what the table would really hand you, so recipes that build their output — dyed armour, a cloned map — come out finished rather than blank.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.in.level: The world whose recipes to search. Recipes are datapack content, so they only exist relative to one.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.in.items: The grid contents, row by row from the top left.
kg.node.mc_crafting_result.in.width: How many columns the items are arranged in.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.tooltip: What a furnace, blast furnace, smoker or campfire would make of an item.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.desc.1: All three answers come from one lookup, because a graph deciding whether to smelt something wants the result, the time and the experience together, and asking separately would search three times.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.note.1: The block is an option rather than four nodes: they ask the same three questions of different tables, and switching furnace for blast furnace should be a flipped option, not a rewiring job.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.note.2: Each block has its own recipes. A smoker takes food and nothing else, so ore in a smoker is not found rather than being an error.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.note.3: Experience is per item and is a fraction — iron pays 0.7 — which is why a furnace hands out whole levels only after several smelts.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.in.level: The world whose recipes to search.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.out.time: How long one item takes, in ticks. 20 ticks is a second.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.out.found: Whether this block has a recipe for that item.
kg.node.mc_smelting_result.option.cookin: Which of the four cooking blocks to ask.
kg.node.mc_recipes_for.tooltip: Every recipe that produces a given item.
kg.node.mc_recipes_for.desc.1: The backwards question — not "what does this make" but "what makes this". Feed an id from here into Recipe Ingredients to find out what it costs.
kg.node.mc_recipes_for.note.1: The expensive one. There is no index from result to recipe, so this walks the whole recipe list: a few thousand entries on a vanilla server, more with mods. Fine in response to something a player did, not every tick.
kg.node.mc_recipes_for.note.2: Sorted by id, because the game stores recipes in a hash map whose order changes between launches. Without sorting, a graph reading the first entry would quietly get a different recipe next time.
kg.node.mc_recipes_for.note.3: Matched on the recipe's declared result. A few recipes compute their output instead of declaring one — map cloning, firework crafting — and those appear under no item at all.
kg.node.mc_recipes_for.in.level: The world whose recipes to search.
kg.node.mc_recipes_for.in.item: The item to find recipes for.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.tooltip: What one named recipe produces, and what kind it is.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.desc.1: For a graph that already knows the recipe — from Recipes For, or written down — and wants its output without reconstructing an input for it.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.note.1: The type is how a graph tells a crafting recipe from a smelting one before deciding where the ingredients should go.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.note.2: This is the recipe's declared output, not an assembled one, because there is no input here to assemble from. A recipe that computes its result gives an empty stack.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.in.level: The world whose recipes to search.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.out.out: What the recipe declares it produces.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.out.type: The recipe kind, e.g. minecraft:crafting or minecraft:smelting.
kg.node.mc_recipe_by_id.out.found: Whether a recipe with that id exists.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.tooltip: What one named recipe needs, one entry per slot.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.desc.1: A shopping list rather than a grid: empty slots in a shaped recipe are skipped, so what comes out is what you have to gather.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.note.1: A slot can accept any of several items — the crafting table takes #minecraft:planks four times, which is one slot with six answers. The list names the first of them and Choices says how many there were, so a graph can see the slot is a tag rather than silently committing to oak.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.note.2: The shape is not reported. A graph that needs it is really trying to fill a table, and Crafting Result answers that from the other end by simply trying the arrangement.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.in.level: The world whose recipes to search.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.out.out: One item per slot that needs something.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.out.choice: How many items each slot would accept, in the same order. Above 1 means the slot is a tag.
kg.node.mc_recipe_ingredients.out.found: Whether a recipe with that id exists.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.tooltip: One roll of a named loot table.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.desc.1: The node for treasure. Chest contents, fishing catches, villager gifts and mob drops are all loot tables, and a command can put them into a container but cannot hand the items to a graph.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.note.1: This rolls dice, so it is the rare data node whose answer changes. Within one run the same node read twice gives one result; across runs it gives new ones. Two independent chest-fulls need two nodes or two runs.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.note.2: Entity and tool are the context most tables ask for: an entity table wants to know who died, a fishing table wants the rod. A chest table needs neither, which is what makes those the simplest case.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.note.3: Server side only, since loot tables live on the server.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.in.level: The world to roll in. Must be a server world.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.in.table: The loot table id, e.g. minecraft:chests/simple_dungeon.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.in.pos: Where the roll is happening. Some tables use it.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.in.entity: The entity involved, if the table wants one.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.in.tool: The tool involved, if the table wants one.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.out.found: Whether a table with that id exists.
kg.node.mc_loot_table_roll.out.ok: False when the table could not be rolled with the context given.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.tooltip: What breaking the block at a position would drop.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.desc.1: The tool is the whole point. Stone with a pickaxe is cobblestone, stone with a hand is nothing, and a silk-touched or fortune-enchanted tool changes the answer again.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.note.1: Reads the block actually at the position rather than taking a state, because the answer depends on more than the state: a shulker box drops its contents and a spawner drops nothing, and both of those live in the block entity.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.note.2: The harvest check is not part of the loot table — the game makes it separately, before rolling. This node makes it too, which is why a bare hand on stone reports nothing rather than cobblestone. Harvestable is that check's result.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.note.3: An empty list is a real answer: air drops nothing, and so does the wrong tool. Harvestable is what tells the two apart.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.in.level: The world to read. Must be a server world.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.in.tool: What it is being broken with. An empty stack means bare hands.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.in.entity: Who is breaking it, if the table cares.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.out.state: The block state that was read.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.out.harvestable: Whether this tool is good enough to drop anything at all.
kg.node.mc_block_drops.out.ok: False when there is no server world, or no position.
kg.node.mc_add_enchantment.tooltip: A copy of the stack with an enchantment added or raised.
kg.node.mc_add_enchantment.desc.1: A data node rather than an action, like every other stack operation: it returns a new stack and changes nothing, so it composes in an expression. Nothing is written to the world until that stack is put somewhere.
kg.node.mc_add_enchantment.note.1: No validity checking, deliberately. The game itself lets commands put any enchantment on any item, and a blueprint is closer to a command than to an enchanting table — a level above the normal maximum works, exactly as the enchant command allows.
kg.node.mc_add_enchantment.in.level: The world, for resolving the identifier.
kg.node.mc_add_enchantment.out.ok: False for an unknown identifier, an empty stack, or a level of zero.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.tooltip: A copy of the stack with one enchantment taken off.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.desc.1: The other half of Add Enchantment, which had no counterpart: a graph could enchant a tool and never un-enchant it. A data node like its opposite — it returns a new stack and changes nothing.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.note.1: Reports what it changed, not what it attempted: removing an enchantment the item did not have is false, and so is an unknown id, because neither altered the stack.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.note.2: Removing the last enchantment leaves a plain item rather than one with an empty enchantment list, so the result compares equal to a stack that was never enchanted.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.note.3: Needs a world, like everything else here: enchantments became a datapack registry in 1.21, so an id only means something relative to a loaded world.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.in.stack: The stack to base the copy on.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.in.level: The world whose enchantment registry to look in.
kg.node.mc_remove_enchantment.out.ok: False when the item did not have it, or the id is unknown.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_info.tooltip: Reads properties off a block entity.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_info.desc.1: Add a Field block to it and pick a property — its position, its block state and everything else it exposes. Properties are discovered automatically, so this one node covers all of them.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_info.in.target: The value every field block on this node reads.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_position.desc.1: The block it is attached to. Note that a double chest is two block entities side by side, not one wide one — this gives the half you are holding, so a graph iterating chests sees each half separately.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_state.tooltip: The state of the block it belongs to.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_state.desc.1: The full state, so its properties are readable — which way a chest faces, whether a furnace is lit.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_level.tooltip: The level the block entity lives in.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_level.desc.1: Closes a loop: a block entity found by Get Block Entity can hand back its own level, which then feeds a Level Info context or another world query — without the graph carrying the level along beside it.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_level.note.1: A block entity can exist without a level, such as one deserialized from an item, so check Present before using the level.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_level.out.presen: True when the block entity has a level.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_identity.tooltip: Which kind of block entity this is, and whether it has been removed.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_identity.desc.1: The type is a registry identifier, so it compares directly against an Identifier constant.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_identity.note.1: Removed means the block is gone but this object is still referenced somewhere. Reading its contents afterwards gives stale data, so a graph holding one across ticks should check.
kg.node.mc_block_entity_identity.out.rem: True once the block entity has been removed.
kg.node.mc_item_in_tag.out.out: Whether the item is in the tag.
kg.node.mc_nbt_keys.tooltip: The keys a compound tag contains, how many, and whether it is empty.
kg.node.mc_nbt_keys.desc.1: The piece the other NBT nodes could not express. Get and Has answer questions about a key you already know; this is how a graph walks a tag it did not write — feed the keys into a For Each and read each value with NBT Get.
kg.node.mc_nbt_keys.note.1: The key list is sorted. Minecraft's own tag storage is a hash map, so its natural order is arbitrary between two tags with identical contents; sorting makes this output a function of the value, which matters if a graph compares or renders it.
kg.node.mc_nbt_keys.out.size: How many entries the tag has.
kg.node.mc_nbt_keys.out.empty: True when the tag has no entries.
kg.node.mc_nbt_set.out.out: A copy with the value stored.
kg.node.mc_nbt_entity.tooltip: Serialises an entity to its NBT compound.
kg.node.mc_nbt_entity.desc.1: The entity counterpart of Block Entity NBT, and the way to reach state that has no dedicated block: a horse's jump strength, a villager's trades, a modded mob's custom fields. Those live on subclasses that no shared property block could reach.
kg.node.mc_nbt_entity.note.1: Without the id, so the tag describes what the entity is rather than which entity it is — it can be written onto another entity of the same type.
kg.node.mc_get_block_state.out.out: The block state at that position.
kg.node.mc_is_empty_block.out.out: Whether the position holds no block.
kg.node.convert_instanceof.tooltip: Whether a value could be cast to a chosen type.
kg.node.convert_instanceof.desc.1: Cast's question, asked without the answer being fatal — Cast throws when the value does not fit, so this is the guard to put in front of one, or the test to branch on when a wire may carry one of several things. Uses the same check Cast does, including its coercions, so it never says no to something Cast would accept. A missing value is false for every type.
kg.node.mc_item_components.tooltip: Every component id present on a stack.
kg.node.mc_item_components.desc.1: For discovering what a stack carries rather than guessing ids. Feed it into For Each to walk them.
kg.node.mc_fluid_components.tooltip: Every component id present on a fluid stack.
kg.node.mc_fluid_components.desc.1: Fluid stacks carry components too, the same way item stacks do.
kg.node.mc_item_has_component.tooltip: Whether a stack carries a component.
kg.node.mc_item_has_component.desc.1: Presence only, without reading the value — which is how to tell a component that is absent from one whose value happens to be a default.
kg.node.mc_item_has_component.in.compone: The component's id, such as minecraft:damage.
kg.node.mc_item_get_component.tooltip: Reads one component off a stack, as NBT and as text.
kg.node.mc_item_get_component.desc.1: A component's type depends on which component it is, so the exchange goes through the serialised form — the same text that appears in a give command. Values that are not compounds (a bare number for damage, a string for a name) are wrapped under a value key so the NBT output is always usable.
kg.node.mc_item_get_component.in.compone: The component's id, such as minecraft:damage.
kg.node.mc_item_get_component.out.nbt: The value as NBT, ready for the NBT nodes.
kg.node.mc_item_get_component.out.text: The value in its command form.
kg.node.mc_item_get_component.out.found: Whether the stack carries that component.
kg.node.mc_item_set_component.tooltip: Stores one component on a copy of the stack.
kg.node.mc_item_set_component.desc.1: Round-tripping the output of Get Component straight back through here always works, which is what makes the pair usable. An unknown id or NBT that does not fit the component reports ok = false and passes the stack through untouched.
kg.node.mc_item_set_component.in.compone: The component's id, such as minecraft:damage.
kg.node.mc_item_set_component.in.nbt: The value to store, as NBT.
kg.node.mc_item_set_component.out.out: The stack with the component set.
kg.node.mc_item_set_component.out.ok: Whether the id was known and the value fit.
kg.node.mc_item_remove_component.tooltip: Removes one component from a copy of the stack.
kg.node.mc_item_remove_component.desc.1: Removing a component a stack does not have is not an error; the stack comes through unchanged.
kg.node.mc_item_remove_component.in.comp: The component's id, such as minecraft:damage.
kg.node.mc_entity_as_player.tooltip: An entity as a player, when it is one.
kg.node.mc_entity_as_player.desc.1: A player flows down an entity wire freely, but going back the other way needs a check — an entity might not be one. Branch on ok rather than assuming; the generic Cast node's answer to a mismatch is to throw, which is not something a graph can recover from.
kg.node.mc_entity_as_player.out.ok: Whether the entity was a player.
kg.node.mc_entity_is_living.tooltip: Whether an entity has health, effects and equipment at all.
kg.node.mc_entity_is_living.desc.1: Ask before reading living-entity data, so that a health read on an armour stand is a deliberate skip rather than a silent zero. There is no separate living-entity pin type — the nodes that need one check internally and return the neutral answer.
kg.node.mc_entity_is_living.out.out: Whether it is a living entity.
kg.node.mc_direction_opposite.tooltip: The direction facing the other way.
kg.node.mc_direction_opposite.desc.1: A real node rather than an info property because it is reached for constantly, and reading one property through an info block costs the whole graph its static cycle-detection fast path.
kg.node.mc_direction_axis.tooltip: Which axis the direction lies along.
kg.node.mc_direction_axis.desc.1: Typed as an axis rather than the x/y/z string an earlier version produced — the typed form feeds Turn directly, and still shows as text on a String pin because anything coerces to String.

rendertypegraph.warn.vertex_element_defa: A default uses vertex attribute '%s' (not in the format) — using a constant

kg.node.ldlib2_ui_load_xml.tooltip: A UI xml file, loaded by resource id.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_load_xml.desc.1: The file may contain a <root> tree, inline <style> blocks and <stylesheet> references — the whole document format.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_load_xml.in.location: The resource id of the xml file.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_load_xml.out.ui: The loaded UI. Empty if the file was missing.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_load_xml.out.root: The UI's root element, for convenience.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_load_xml.note.1: The client looks in assets, the server in datapacks. A UI both sides build needs its xml under data/, or the server silently builds an empty tree.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_parse_xml.tooltip: UI xml written inline, with as little ceremony as you like.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_parse_xml.desc.1: All three of these mean the same thing: the full <ui><root>…</root></ui>, just <root>…</root>, or bare elements like <button id="ok"/>.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_parse_xml.example.1: <button id="save" class="primary"/> builds one button with an id and a class — enough for a stylesheet and a selector to find it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_create.tooltip: A UI from a root element and the stylesheets it should use.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_create.in.stylesheets: Stylesheets to style the whole tree with.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_create.note.1: A UI is immutable once made. To add a stylesheet later, use Global Stylesheet on the Modular UI.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_create_sized.tooltip: A UI that sizes itself against the screen.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_create_sized.desc.1: The size is recomputed every time the screen initialises, so it survives a window resize — which a fixed layout width would not.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_create_sized.option.mo: How width and height are read.
Pixels subtracted from the screen — a margin on each axis.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_unpack.tooltip: The root element and stylesheets of a UI.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_to_template.tooltip: A snapshot of a UI, as a template.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_to_template.desc.1: Takes either a UI or a bare element — whichever is wired. A template is the form that survives a save file or a packet.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_to_template.note.1: A template stores the tree, ids, classes and persisted fields. Event listeners, sync values and RPCs are Java objects and do not survive.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_load.tooltip: A template from LDLib2's UI resource library.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_load.in.path: A typed path, e.g. builtin(ldlib2:missing), file(/my_ui.ui) or pack(mymod:ui/machine).
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_load.out.ok: False when the path did not resolve; the template output is then the red 'Missing' placeholder.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_create_ui.too: A fresh UI stamped out of a template.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_create_ui.des: Each pass through builds a new tree, so this inside a loop produces one per iteration.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_init.tooltip: Stamps a template into an element that already exists.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_init.desc.1: Unlike Template To UI, this fills a root you already hold — which is what you want when the element is already parented into a bigger tree.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_styles.in.bui: An inline LSS block stored inside the template itself.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_styles.in.sty: Resource ids of stylesheets the template should reference.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_copy.tooltip: An independent copy of a template.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_template_copy.desc.1: A template's NBT is mutable, so two UIs stamped from one that a graph then edited would disagree about what they were stamped from.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_modular_create.tooltip: A live UI instance for a player.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_modular_create.desc.1: This does not mount the tree. It sets up the sync manager, the style engine and the layout tree; the root is attached only when the host says so — a menu on the server, screen init on the client. Until then no element has a Modular UI and nothing has reached the sync manager.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_modular_create.note.1: So sync values reach the manager in the order the tree is walked as it mounts, not the order the graph declared them in. Still deterministic, and still requires both sides to build the same tree.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_new.tooltip: A new element of a registered type.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_new.desc.1: The type list is LDLib2's element registry — the same table an xml tag name resolves through, so 'button' here and <button/> in xml build the same thing.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_new.in.id: The id, for selectors and stylesheets to find it by. Optional.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_new.in.classes: Space-separated class names, as in a class="a b" attribute.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_new.option.typ: Which registered element type to build.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_new.note.1: An exec node, not a plain value: an element has identity, so when it is made has to be something the graph states. Inside a loop it makes a new one per iteration; outside, it makes one that event handlers can find again.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_from_xml.toolt: Elements written as xml — <button id="ok"/> is enough.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_from_xml.out.e: The first element. The common case.
All of them, so a fragment naming several siblings loses nothing.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_add_child.tooltip: Adds a child to a parent.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_add_child.in.index: Where to insert. -1 appends. Sibling order is what a flex layout lays out in.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_add_child.out.out: The parent again, so a build chain can keep threading it along.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_add_child.note.1: Refuses to create a cycle — adding an element to its own descendant would make hit-testing loop forever.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_add_children.tooltip: Adds every element of a list to a parent, in order.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_remove_child.tooltip: Removes a child from its parent.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_remove_self.tooltip: Removes an element from whatever parent it has.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_clear_children.in.keep: Keep the element's own internal children. On by default, and usually right: a Button owns its caption, a Scroller owns its handle, and clearing those leaves a control that can never display anything again.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_copy.tooltip: An independent copy of an element and everything under it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_copy.note.1: The copy carries the tree, ids, classes and persisted fields — but not event listeners, sync values or RPCs, which NBT cannot hold. Attach behaviour after copying, not before.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_deserialize.tooltip: Loads an NBT tree into an element, replacing what was there.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_descendants.tooltip: Every element under this one, depth-first.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_descendants.in.include: Whether the element itself is in the list.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_ancestor_of_type.toolt: The nearest ancestor of a chosen element type.
How a child finds the panel it lives in without the graph having to carry a wire all the way down.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_select.tooltip: Elements matching a selector, searched downwards from a root.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_select.in.selector: The same syntax LSS uses: #id, .class, a bare type name, or a combination.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_select.out.first: The first match, since most selectors are meant to find one thing.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_select.note.1: Walks the tree, so it works before the UI is mounted — which is when a build needs it. Find By Id is faster but only sees mounted elements.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_select_regex.tooltip: Elements whose id matches a regular expression.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_select_regex.desc.1: For rows a template numbered slot_0, slot_1, …: slot_\d+ gets all of them without knowing how many there are.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_find_by_id.tooltip: An element by id, through the live UI's index.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_find_by_id.note.1: A map lookup rather than a tree walk, but it only sees elements already added to the UI. During a build there is nothing to find.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_id.desc.1: The id is the handle a selector, a stylesheet rule and Find By Id all use.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_flag.tooltip: Flips one of an element's state flags.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_flag.option.flag.t: Drawn or not. An invisible element still takes up its layout space and still receives events.
Receives events or not. Off is what 'disabled' means.
In the layout or not. Off removes it entirely, so siblings close the gap.
Whether content outside the element's bounds is drawn rather than clipped.
Whether the mouse can hit it. Off makes it click-through.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_focus.option.op.toolti: What to do with the focus.
Give this element focus. It must be focusable.
Take focus away from this element, if it has it.
Drop focus entirely, whatever holds it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_focus.note.1: Focus lives on the live UI, so this does nothing for an element that has not been mounted yet. Focusing is nearly always a handler's job, not a build step.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_text.tooltip: Sets the caption of anything that shows one.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_text.desc.1: Covers Label, Text, Button and Text Field. For a Text Field the component is flattened to a plain string.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_get_value.tooltip: The element's own value — a Toggle's boolean, a Slider's float, an Item Slot's stack.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_get_value.option.value: Types the output pin. Leaving it unknown gives an anything-goes pin and still works.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_value.tooltip: Writes the element's value through its own setter, so listeners and bindings see it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_value.in.notify: Whether listeners are told. Turn it off to write a value back into the control that produced it without re-entering your own change handler.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_property.tooltip: Writes one of the element's configurable fields.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_property.desc.1: The property list is exactly what LDLib2's own UI editor shows in its Inspector, and the value pin takes the field's declared type — pick progress-bar then value and it becomes a float pin.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_property.option.el: Which element type's property list to offer. Only a lens for the picker — the write itself uses whatever element arrives.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_property.note.1: Writes go through the field's annotated setter when it has one, which is where the behaviour lives — clamping a progress value, notifying a toggle's listeners.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_set_property.note.2: Appearance is not here. Everything visual goes through Set Lss and Classes instead.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_get_property.tooltip: Reads one of the element's configurable fields.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_list_properties.toolti: The configurable property names an element has.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_info.tooltip: Holds one element for the property blocks placed inside it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_element_info.desc.1: Wire the element once, then stack as many property blocks as you need — instead of wiring the same element into a dozen separate nodes.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_identity.tooltip: The element's id, type name and classes.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_interaction.toolt: Whether the mouse is over it and whether it holds focus.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_interaction.out.s: True when the cursor is over this element or anything inside it — what a container usually wants to know.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_structure.tooltip: Where the element sits in the tree.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_position.tooltip: The element's position, relative to its parent's content box.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_size.tooltip: The element's own width and height, border included.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_content_box.toolt: The box children are laid out in: inside the padding.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_margin.tooltip: The element's margins, one per side.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_info_position.note.1: Layout numbers only exist once a client has laid the tree out. On the server, and before the first layout pass, they read zero — so read them in a hover or tick handler, not during the build.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_set.tooltip: Sets one LSS property on one element.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_set.desc.1: The value is written the way LSS writes it, because the same parser reads it: #ff5555, 50%, 12, center. A number is formatted plainly; an integer wired into a colour property becomes #AARRGGBB.
Which layer of the cascade the value belongs to. Higher layers win: default < stylesheet < inline < animation < important.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_set.note.1: Prefer Classes when a stylesheet could describe the look. Reach for this when the value is one only the graph can know — a bar width computed from a number.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_remove.tooltip: Removes a property this graph set, letting what was underneath show through.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_remove.desc.1: Only removes the graph's own value at that layer — a stylesheet rule setting the same property is untouched. That is how a hover effect is undone without erasing the element's normal appearance.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_block.tooltip: A whole LSS declaration block at once: color: #ff5555; opacity: 0.5;
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_block.desc.1: Exactly what a UI xml file's style="…" attribute means, parsed by the same code. Unknown property names are skipped rather than failing the block.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_get.tooltip: The value an element's style resolves to right now.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_lss_get.desc.1: Answers after the whole cascade — a colour coming from a stylesheet reads the same as one set inline. Good for checking a style, poor for storing the graph's own state in.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_class.tooltip: Adds, removes, replaces or toggles class names.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_class.desc.1: The pipeline most interaction should use. A handler that adds .selected leaves what 'selected' looks like with the designer, works for every element the rule matches, and is undone by removing one name.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_class.in.classes: Space-separated names, as in a class="a b" attribute.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_class.option.op.toolti: What to do with the names.
Replace the whole class list with them. With no names, clears every class.
Add each one that is absent, remove each one that is present.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_has_class.tooltip: Whether an element carries a class name.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_parse.toolt: Parses LSS text into a stylesheet.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_parse.in.na: A name for the sheet, shown in the UI debugger.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_load.toolti: A stylesheet from a resource id.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_load.desc.1: ldlib2:lss/mc.lss is that one file. ldlib2:lss/mc — no extension — is every lss/mc.lss in every loaded pack, merged.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_builtin.opt: Which one. The merged variants also pick up rules other packs contribute at the same path, which is what makes a theme extensible.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_merge.toolt: Merges one stylesheet's rules into another, in place.
Mutates the target. Merging into a sheet the manager owns edits it for every UI in the game — merge into one this graph parsed.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_register.to: Registers a stylesheet under a resource id, so anything can load it by name.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_stylesheet_register.no: Global and permanent for the session. A graph that runs more than once should register the same id each time rather than generating names.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_local_stylesheet.toolt: A stylesheet scoped to one element and its descendants.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_local_stylesheet.in.ls: Raw LSS text, if you would rather not build a stylesheet first. The parsed stylesheet input wins if both are wired.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_local_stylesheet.optio: Attach, detach, or remove every local sheet.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_global_stylesheet.tool: Adds or removes a stylesheet on a live UI.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_global_stylesheet.desc: The only way to add a sheet after the UI was constructed, because a UI is immutable. This is what runtime theming uses.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_global_stylesheet.note: Client only — the server has no style engine.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_apply_stylesheet.toolt: Matches a stylesheet against an element and writes the matching rules onto it, by hand.
The step the style engine does automatically when an element joins a client UI. Doing it explicitly is useful where there is no engine — on the server — or not one yet, before the UI is mounted.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_apply_stylesheet.in.re: Whether descendants are matched too. On by default, since a stylesheet's selectors are meant to find things throughout a subtree.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_animate.tooltip: Interpolates a style property from where it is now to a target.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_animate.note.1: Client only, and only on a mounted element — the animation engine lives on the live UI.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_animate.note.2: The animation outranks stylesheet and inline values while it runs, then leaves its final value behind as an inline one. To hand the property back to the stylesheet afterwards, remove it with Remove Lss at the inline layer.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_tooltip.tooltip: Sets the tooltip lines an element shows on hover.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_tooltip.in.line: A single line — the common case, and shorter than building a list.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_tooltip.in.lines: More lines, appended after the single one.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_tooltip.desc.1: An empty list clears the tooltip, which is how a hint is turned off once it no longer applies.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_event.tooltip: Runs a chain whenever an event reaches an element.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_event.desc.1: Two exec outputs. 'next' continues building the UI straight away; 'onEvent' runs every time the player triggers the event, however much later.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_event.desc.2: The handler is evaluated fresh each time, so whatever it reads from the UI is current rather than whatever was true while the tree was being built.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_event.in.useCapture: Listen on the way down instead of the way up. An event travels root to target, fires, then travels back — a capture listener sees it before any descendant does, which is how a dialog intercepts clicks meant for what is underneath.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_event.option.eventT: Which event. The list is LDLib2's built-in types, but anything you type is accepted — a custom type dispatched by another graph is not in any registry.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_event.example.1: New Element (button) → On Event (mouseClick) → onEvent → Classes (toggle 'selected'). One node registers, one reacts.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_server_event.toolti: Runs a chain on the server whenever an event reaches the element on the client.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_server_event.desc.1: For a reaction that has to change the world — consume an item, flip a machine — where the client has nothing real to change.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_server_event.note.1: The event is rebuilt from the wire: coordinates, button and key data survive; drag state and custom data do not.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_server_event.note.2: There is a round trip, so the server reacts a tick or so later. Anything the player must see immediately belongs in a client handler.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_server_event.note.3: Registers an RPC, so both sides must reach this node in the same order as every other sync registration. Build the same tree on both sides.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_tick.tooltip: Runs a chain once per tick, while the element is active and displayed.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_tick.desc.1: The hook for anything that has to poll: a countdown, a value that changes without an input event.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_tick.note.1: Twenty times a second, and it recomputes the chain each time. Keep it small — a value that changes rarely belongs on a sync value's onReceived instead.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_info.tooltip: Everything carried by a dispatched event.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_info.out.x: Horizontal position, in the target element's own space — so it can be compared against the element's content box without transforming anything.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_info.out.y: Vertical position, in the target element's own space.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_info.out.charact: The character typed, for a charTyped event. Empty when none.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_info.out.related: The other element involved: on focus, the one that lost it; on blur, the one that gained it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_stop.desc.1: How a handler says 'I dealt with it'. Without it, a click on a button inside a scrollable panel also reaches the panel.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_stop.option.mode: No further element sees it, in either direction.
As above, and no other listener on this element runs either.
This element's other listeners still run; nothing after this phase does.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_dispatch.tooltip: Builds an event and dispatches it at an element, as though the player had caused it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_dispatch.desc.1: Two uses: synthetic input, and a custom event type as a message bus — dispatch mymod:refresh at the root and let every part of the UI that cares listen for it, instead of wiring each one to the thing that changed.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_event_dispatch.in.send: Whether server-side listeners are notified too. Off by default: a synthetic event claiming the player did something is worth thinking about before it reaches the server.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.tooltip: A value LDLib2 keeps the same on both sides.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.desc.1: Use a sync value for state — what is this now — and an RPC for a moment, when something just happened.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.desc.2: Wire something into 'source' and the sending side pulls that expression every tick, so the value tracks it. Leave it unwired and push with Set Synced instead.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.in.element: The element that owns it. The value lives as long as that element is in the UI.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.in.name: A name, for debugging. The wire does not carry it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.option.valu: What is being synced. Must be a concrete type — the sync layer needs an accessor to turn it into bytes.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.option.dire: Server to client. The usual one: the server owns the truth, the client shows it.
Client to server. For what the player edits.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_value.note.1: The wire identifies a sync value by the order it was registered in, not by its name. Both sides must register the same values in the same sequence — so build the same tree on both sides, and never branch the structure on Which Side.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_get.tooltip: The value a sync value currently holds, on whichever side asks.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_set.tooltip: Writes a sync value, so the other side sees it next tick.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_sync_set.in.markChange: Force a send even when nothing looks changed. Needed for a value edited in place — a list, a tag — because the dirty check compares against the very instance that was mutated.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_binding.tooltip: A two-way binding between a server-side value and an element.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_binding.desc.1: Goes one step further than a sync value: bound to an element, an Item Slot shows the server's stack and a Text Field sends what the player types, with no handler in between.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_binding.desc.2: For some elements it is the only way in — an Item Slot's real contents are not a configurable field and cannot be reached with Set Property.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_binding.in.serverValue: What the server side provides. Pulled every tick, so the binding tracks whatever expression is wired here.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_binding.note.1: 'onReceived' fires on whichever side an update lands on. The binding only moves the value — reacting to it is the graph's job.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_bind.tooltip: Attaches a binding to an element.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_bind.note.1: Only works on an element that carries a value — Item Slot, Fluid Slot, Progress Bar, Toggle, Slider, Text Field, Selector, Label and the rest. Anything else reports false; use a sync value and a handler instead.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_unbind.tooltip: Detaches a binding, so the element stops mirroring it.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_define.tooltip: Declares a call the other side can make, and runs a chain when it does.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_define.option.argC: How many arguments, up to four. Beyond that, send a compound tag with On Message instead.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_define.option.retu: What the call answers with. Leave it unknown for a one-way call.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_define.note.1: To answer, end the onCall chain at Rpc Return.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_define.note.2: Both sides must register the same RPCs in the same order — the wire carries a registration index, not a name.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_return.tooltip: Answers the RPC call currently being handled.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_return.in.rpc: Leave unwired to answer the innermost call, which is what a handler wants unless it is nested inside another.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_send.tooltip: Calls an RPC on the other side.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_send.desc.1: 'next' continues immediately; 'onReturn' fires when the answer arrives, at least a tick later. A graph that needs the answer must continue from onReturn.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_rpc_send.note.1: The argument types must match the defining node's, position for position — the wire carries no names.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_message.tooltip: Runs a chain when the other side sends a named message to this element.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_on_message.desc.1: The zero-configuration path: no types to line up, and the payload is a compound tag the graph's NBT nodes can take apart. Start here before reaching for a typed RPC.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_send_message.tooltip: Sends a named message with an NBT payload to the same element on the other side.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_side.tooltip: Which side this evaluation is running on.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_side.desc.1: Derived from the current thread, so it answers correctly even before a UI exists.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_side.note.1: Branch on this for behaviour — only the server can change the world, only the client can animate. Never branch the shape of the UI tree or the set of sync values on it: those are matched across the network by registration order.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_modular_of.tooltip: The live UI an element belongs to.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_modular_of.out.mounted: False until the element has been added to a mounted tree.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_mui_info.tooltip: Everything about a live UI a graph is likely to ask for.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_mui_info.out.tick: The UI's own tick counter, starting at zero when it opened — which is what a timeout in a UI wants to measure against.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_close.desc.1: Goes through the player's container, which is the one action a menu-backed UI and a plain screen both agree on.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_start_drag.tooltip: Begins a drag, carrying an arbitrary payload.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_start_drag.desc.1: Call it from a mouseDown handler on whatever the player grabbed. A drag does not begin because the mouse moved — it begins because something started one.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_start_drag.in.payload: Anything the graph carries — an item stack, an index, the source element itself. It comes back out of Drag Info on whatever receives the drop.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_start_drag.note.1: Needs a mounted element: the drag lives on the live UI, so there is nowhere to start one before the tree is attached.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_start_drag.note.2: Client only. LDLib2 never sends drag events to the server — have the drop handler send an RPC or a message once it knows what was dropped.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_drag_info.tooltip: What is being dragged, read off a drag event.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_drag_info.desc.1: The dragged object lives on the event's drag handler rather than on the event, which is why Event Info cannot reach it and this node exists.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_drag_info.in.element: An alternative to the event: a tick or mouseMove handler has no drag event to hand, but can still ask its UI whether a drag is in progress.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_drag_info.out.payload: Untyped, exactly as it was given. A handler expecting a particular type should check rather than assume.
kg.node.ldlib2_ui_drag_info.out.source: The element the drag started from — what dragEnd is dispatched at.
kg.node.rt_color.option.mode.tooltip: Which editor to use: the standard 0..1 color picker, or an HDR picker with an extra intensity.
kg.node.rt_color.option.color.tooltip: The color, with components in 0..1. Kept even while HDR mode is active, so switching back does not lose it.
kg.node.rt_color.option.hdr_color.toolti: The HDR color: a base color plus an intensity that is premultiplied into RGB when baked, so components may exceed 1 for emission or bloom.
kg.node.rt_curve.option.curve.tooltip: The curve itself: cubic bezier segments drawn in the curve editor, plus the output range they are remapped to.
kg.node.rt_gradient.option.gradient.tool: The gradient itself: color keys and alpha keys on separate tracks, with Blend or Fixed interpolation.
kg.node.rt_scene_depth.option.sampling.t: How the sampled depth is expressed: Linear01 (0 near to 1 far), Raw (hardware depth) or Eye (world-unit distance from the camera).
kg.node.rt_screen_position.option.mode.t: Which screen-space coordinate system to report: Default (0..1), Raw (homogeneous, W is the eye distance), Center, Tiled or Pixel.
kg.node.rt_vertex_color.option.mode.tool: How the vertex color is lit: Mix Light (vanilla per-vertex diffuse), Color (raw and unlit) or Block (multiplied by the baked lightmap).
kg.node.rt_and.out.out: True when both input is true.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.cylindricalVerte: Not used on this version: Minecraft 1.21.1 has a single linear fog band, so this port exists only so graphs stay compatible with versions that have more. Wiring it changes nothing.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.renderDistanceSt: Not used on this version: Minecraft 1.21.1 has a single linear fog band, so this port exists only so graphs stay compatible with versions that have more. Wiring it changes nothing.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.in.renderDistanceEn: Not used on this version: Minecraft 1.21.1 has a single linear fog band, so this port exists only so graphs stay compatible with versions that have more. Wiring it changes nothing.
kg.node.rt_apply_fog.out.out: The input color blended toward the fog color.
kg.node.rt_blend.out.out: The two colors combined, faded from the base by opacity.
kg.node.rt_channel_mask.out.out: The color with the unselected channels zeroed.
kg.node.rt_channel_mixer.out.out: The color with each channel rebuilt from the weighted mix.
kg.node.rt_checkerboard.out.out: The checker pattern, in the two chosen colors.
kg.node.rt_colorspace_conversion.out.out: The color in the target space.
kg.node.rt_contrast.out.out: The color pushed away from or pulled toward mid-grey.
kg.node.rt_cross.out.out: A vector perpendicular to both inputs, whose length is the area of the parallelogram they span.
kg.node.rt_distance.out.out: The straight-line distance between the two points.
kg.node.rt_dither.out.out: The input minus the ordered pattern; feed it to Alpha Discard to turn a fade into a stipple.
kg.node.rt_dot.out.out: How much the two vectors agree: for unit vectors, the cosine of the angle between them.
kg.node.rt_ellipse.out.out: A mask: 1 inside the ellipse, 0 outside.
kg.node.rt_exp.out.out: The base raised to the input, channel by channel.
kg.node.rt_flipbook.out.out: The uv remapped into the current cell of the sprite sheet.
kg.node.rt_fresnel.out.out: Near 0 where the surface faces you, rising toward 1 at grazing angles.
kg.node.rt_hue.out.out: The color rotated around the hue wheel.
kg.node.rt_inverse_lerp.in.a: The value that corresponds to a blend factor of 0.
kg.node.rt_inverse_lerp.in.b: The value that corresponds to a blend factor of 1.
kg.node.rt_inverse_lerp.in.t: The value to locate between a and b.
kg.node.rt_inverse_lerp.out.out: The blend factor that would produce t; 0 at a, 1 at b, and outside 0..1 beyond them.
kg.node.rt_invert_colors.out.out: The color with the selected channels inverted.
kg.node.rt_log.in.a: The value to take the logarithm of.
kg.node.rt_log.out.out: The logarithm in the chosen base, channel by channel.
kg.node.rt_mat4_determinant.out.out: The determinant; 0 means the matrix has no inverse.
kg.node.rt_mat4_transform.in.v: The vector to transform; w = 1 for a position, w = 0 for a direction.
kg.node.rt_mat4_transpose.out.out: The matrix with rows and columns swapped.
